a: The LORD spoke to Moses.
p: Chapters 25–31 are built from seven speeches of God. The seventh is about the Sabbath.
b: The instructions for the tabernacle come in seven speeches, each opening "The LORD spoke to Moses" (or "said") (25:1; 30:11; 30:17; 30:22; 30:34; 31:1; 31:12). The seventh and last is about the Sabbath (31:12–17). Peter Kearney and others have argued that the seven speeches were shaped to echo the seven days of Genesis 1, so that building God's dwelling is pictured as a new creation. Others think the pattern is looser than that. Either way, the section begins and ends with God speaking, and it ends where creation ends, with rest. See also the note on 39:43.

a: set aside a gift for me
t: A gift lifted off for God
p: Terumah means something lifted off your goods and set apart. It gives this Torah portion its name.
b: The Hebrew terumah comes from a verb meaning "lift up." It is a portion lifted off from what a person owns and set apart for God. The synagogue reading for 25:1–27:19 is called Terumah. The gift is free: only those "whose heart urges him on" give. The verb "urges him on" (yidvennu) is related to nedavah, the "freewill offering" of 35:29. The book shows two collections of gold side by side. For the calf, Aaron asks and the people hand over their earrings at once (32:2–3). For the tabernacle, they give so much that Moses has to tell them to stop (36:3–7).

a: violet, purple and scarlet yarn
t: The costliest colors in the world
p: Blue and purple dye came from sea snails and cost a fortune. Israel's tent was dressed like a royal house.
b: Tekhelet (blue or blue-violet) and argaman (red-purple) were made from the glands of murex sea snails, an industry famous along the Phoenician coast. Thousands of snails gave a few grams of dye, so these colors were worn by kings. "Scarlet" is literally "worm of crimson," a red dye from the dried bodies of an insect that lives on oak trees. The same three colors and fine linen run through the tabernacle, the veil and the high priest's clothes. Menahem Haran noted that the materials grow costlier the closer one comes to the ark: bronze outside, silver at the bases, gold inside. Blue thread later marked every Israelite's tassels (Numbers 15:38).

a: fine leather
t: Dolphins, sea cows or fine leather?
p: No one knows what a tachash was. Guesses range from dolphins to a one-horned animal.
b: The outer covering is made of tachash skins. The KJV guessed "badgers' skins." Many scholars compare an Arabic word for the dugong, a sea cow of the Red Sea, hence "dolphin" or "porpoise" skins (as in the word list). Others link it to an Egyptian word for working leather, so "fine leather" (BSB) or "durable leather." The Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus, took it as a color: "skins dyed blue." The Talmud (Shabbat 28b) records a view that the tachash was a beautiful, many-colored animal with one horn that existed only in Moses' day. The Plain English gives the most cautious meaning.

a: I will live in their midst
p: The verb shakhan, 'to dwell, settle,' gives the words mishkan (tabernacle) and Shekhinah (God's presence).
b: The point of the whole building is in this verse. God does not say "I will live in it" but "I will live in their midst," in the middle of the people, and many Jewish teachers have drawn the lesson that the people, not the building, are God's true home. The verb shakhan means to settle or camp. From it come mishkan, the word translated "tabernacle" (25:9), and the later rabbinic word Shekhinah, God's dwelling presence. Targum Onkelos, the Aramaic translation read in synagogues, renders: "I will make my Shekhinah rest among them." John 1:14 uses the matching Greek verb: "the Word became flesh and pitched his tent (eskēnōsen) among us."

a: the tabernacle
p: The text uses several names for one structure. "Tabernacle" comes from the Latin word for a tent.
b: The structure has several names. Mishkan, "dwelling place," stresses that God lives there. Ohel mo'ed, "tent of meeting" (27:21), stresses that God meets Moses and Israel there. Miqdash, "holy place" or sanctuary (25:8), stresses its holiness, and "the tabernacle of the testimony" (38:21) names it after the tablets kept inside. English "tabernacle" comes from the Latin Vulgate's tabernaculum, "tent, hut." Strictly, mishkan is the inner layer of woven curtains, and the "tent" is the goat-hair layer over it (26:1, 7), but the words are often used for the whole.

a: an ark of acacia wood
p: Aron is an ordinary word for a box or chest. It is not the word used for Noah's ark.
b: Aron means a chest or box. The same word is used for a collection box in the temple (2 Kings 12:9) and for Joseph's coffin (Genesis 50:26). Noah's ark and the basket of baby Moses are a different word, tevah (Genesis 6:14; Exodus 2:3). With a cubit of about 18 inches, the ark was roughly 45 inches long and 27 inches wide and high, about the size of a large chest of drawers laid on its side. Later books call it "the ark of the covenant" (Numbers 10:33; Deuteronomy 10:8), "the ark of God" (1 Samuel 3:3), and here "the ark of the testimony" (25:22).

a: so the ark can be carried by them
p: Egyptian tombs and temples had gilded chests and shrines carried on poles, much like the ark.
b: Carrying chests and shrines on poles was standard in Egypt. Tutankhamun's tomb (about 1325 BC) held a wooden chest topped by the jackal god Anubis, with gilded poles for carrying it, and Egyptian reliefs show priests carrying a god's boat-shrine on poles in procession. Kenneth Kitchen and James Hoffmeier point to these as evidence that the tabernacle's design fits the Late Bronze Age. Michael Homan adds the strongest form of the argument: Ramesses II's war camp at Kadesh (about 1274 BC) had a royal tent in a courtyard with the same two-to-one plan, a layout an exilic writer would hardly have known. Critical scholars reply that military tent camps and portable royal shrines lasted well into the Iron Age, so the parallels show where the idea came from, not when the text was written. When David's men later moved the ark on a cart instead of carrying it, it ended in disaster (2 Samuel 6:3–7; 1 Chronicles 15:13–15).

a: They are never to be taken out.
p: The poles stayed in the rings, and they were still there in Solomon's temple.
b: Only the ark has this rule. The table and altars have poles too, but only the ark's poles must stay in place, perhaps so that no one would need to touch the ark itself (2 Samuel 6:6–7). In Solomon's temple the poles were so long that their ends could be seen from the holy place: "They have stayed there until today" (1 Kings 8:8). Numbers 4:6, where the Levites "put in its poles" before a journey, seems to clash with this verse. Jewish commentators answered that the poles were only adjusted or that the verse means "set in place," while some modern scholars see two different traditions.

a: the testimony that I will give you
p: Edut, 'testimony' or 'witness,' is the stone tablets with the covenant terms.
b: Edut means a testimony, a solemn witness. In Exodus it names the two stone tablets (31:18; 32:15; 34:29), the written terms of the covenant. Ancient treaties worked the same way. A Hittite treaty from the 1300s BC states that a copy has been placed before the sun goddess in her temple, so that the god can watch over the agreement. Israel's covenant copy is kept in the holiest place, beneath God's throne. Later the book of the law was set beside the ark as a witness (Deuteronomy 31:26). Hebrews 9:4 adds a jar of manna and Aaron's staff (Exodus 16:33–34; Numbers 17:10), but 1 Kings 8:9 says that by Solomon's time there was nothing in the ark except the two tablets.

a: an atonement lid
t: Mercy seat, atonement cover, or place of atonement?
p: Kapporet is linked to kipper, 'atone.' Tyndale coined 'mercy seat'; the Greek has hilasterion.
b: The lid of the ark is called kapporet. The word looks like a noun from kipper, "make atonement," and on the Day of Atonement the high priest sprinkles blood on it (Leviticus 16:14–15). Some scholars connect it instead with "cover" (the lid covers the ark), or with an Egyptian word for the sole of the foot, so a footstool. William Tyndale coined "mercy seat" in 1530, following Luther's Gnadenstuhl, and the KJV kept it, but nothing in the Hebrew says "seat." The Septuagint calls it hilastērion, "place or means of atonement." Paul uses that word of Christ (Romans 3:25), and Hebrews 9:5 uses it of the lid. The Plain English "atonement lid" tries to keep both the object and its purpose.

a: two cherubim
p: Biblical cherubim are fierce winged guardians, closer to sphinxes than to the baby angels of later art.
b: The cute winged infants called "cherubs" in later art come from Renaissance painting, not the Bible. In Scripture the keruvim guard the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24), carry God's throne (Ezekiel 1; 10), and are woven into the tabernacle curtains (26:1, 31). Ezekiel's have four faces and four wings (Ezekiel 1:5–11; 10:14). In the art of Israel's neighbors, winged creatures with a lion's body and a human head stand guard beside thrones and temple doors. Many scholars link the word to the Akkadian karibu, a figure who prays or blesses, though the link is debated. The Bible never describes the ark's cherubim in detail.

a: sheltering the lid with their wings
p: The cherubim and the lid make a throne for the invisible God. No image sits on it.
b: Later Scripture calls God the LORD "who sits enthroned on the cherubim" (1 Samuel 4:4; 2 Kings 19:15; Psalm 80:1; 99:1), and calls the ark his footstool (1 Chronicles 28:2; Psalm 132:7). Phoenician carvings show kings sitting on thrones whose sides are winged sphinxes, as on the stone coffin of King Ahiram of Byblos (about 1000 BC). So the ark and its cherubim form a throne with no one visible on it. Israel's God is present but is never shown in an image. This is the background for the shock of the golden calf in 32:4. The Talmud (Bava Batra 99a) says that when Israel did God's will, the cherubim faced each other like loving partners, and when Israel sinned they turned away (2 Chronicles 3:13).
r: 1 Samuel 4:4; 2 Kings 19:15; Psalm 80:1; Psalm 99:1; 1 Chronicles 28:2; 2 Chronicles 3:13; Hebrews 9:5

a: There I will meet you.
p: The verb ya'ad, 'meet by appointment,' gives the name 'tent of meeting.' The ark is a place of speech.
b: The verb no'adti, "I will meet," comes from the root that gives mo'ed, an appointed meeting, as in "tent of meeting" (27:21). The ark is not mainly a box of treasures. It is the spot where God's voice will come from: "from between the two cherubim." Numbers 7:89 shows this happening: Moses goes into the tent and hears the voice speaking to him from above the lid. The tabernacle makes Mount Sinai portable. What Moses heard on the mountain he will now hear in the camp.

a: the Presence Bread
p: The Hebrew is literally 'bread of the face.' The KJV called it 'shewbread.'
b: Lechem panim is literally "bread of the face," bread set out before God's face. Tyndale called it "shewbread," bread put on show. Leviticus 24:5–9 explains that twelve loaves were laid out every Sabbath and the old ones eaten by the priests. In other ancient temples, meals were set before the god's statue as its food. Israel had no statue, and Psalm 50:12–13 mocks the idea that God needs food. David's men once ate this bread in an emergency (1 Samuel 21:1–6), and Jesus used that story to show that human need can come before ritual (Mark 2:25–26). The Talmud (Chagigah 26b) tells that the bread stayed fresh all week.
r: Leviticus 24:5–9; 1 Samuel 21:1–6; Psalm 50:12–13; Mark 2:25–26; Matthew 12:3–4; Hebrews 9:2

a: Make a lampstand of pure gold.
p: The menorah is shaped like a flowering tree. Many see the tree of life in it.
b: The menorah has a trunk, branches, cups, knobs and flowers: it is a stylized tree in blossom. Carol Meyers showed that it fits a long ancient tradition of sacred trees, and many readers see in it the tree of life of Eden (Genesis 2:9), so that the holy place recalls the garden. Its seven lamps burned all night (27:20–21). Zechariah saw a lampstand fed by two olive trees (Zechariah 4:2–14), and in Revelation seven lampstands stand for the churches (Revelation 1:12, 20). The Arch of Titus in Rome (about AD 81) shows Roman soldiers carrying off the temple's menorah after AD 70, and that carving became the model for the emblem of the State of Israel.

a: of hammered work
p: Rashi tells that Moses could not picture the lampstand, so God made it come out of the fire by itself.
b: The lampstand had to be beaten out of a single block of gold ("one piece," 25:36), with no soldered parts. The Hebrew says "the lampstand will be made" rather than "you will make," and Rashi, following the midrash Tanhuma, saw a hint in this: Moses found the design too hard to grasp, so God told him to throw the gold into the fire, and the lampstand came out made. The rabbis also said Moses was puzzled by the lampstand, the new moon and the rules on unclean animals until God showed him each with a finger. The story makes a theological point: the true maker of the sanctuary is God.

a: shaped like almond flowers
p: Shaqed, 'almond,' sounds like shoqed, 'watching.' The almond is the first tree to bloom.
b: In the land of Israel the almond is the first tree to blossom, in late winter, while other trees still sleep. Its name shaqed sounds like shoqed, "keeping watch," a wordplay used in Jeremiah 1:11–12: Jeremiah sees an almond branch, and God says, "I am watching over my word." Aaron's staff, laid before the testimony, sprouted, budded and produced almonds overnight (Numbers 17:8). So the almond lampstand may suggest a God who stays awake and watches, as the lamps burn all night (27:21; Psalm 121:4).

a: Make its seven lamps.
p: Josephus and Philo said the seven lamps stood for the seven planets. Christians saw the Spirit.
b: The number seven runs through the tabernacle story, as it does through creation. Jewish writers of the first century, Philo and Josephus, said the seven lamps stood for the seven moving lights of the sky then known (sun, moon and five planets), so that the tabernacle was a small model of the universe (Josephus, Jewish War 5.217). Zechariah's lampstand has seven lamps that are "the eyes of the LORD" (Zechariah 4:2, 10). Revelation 4:5 sees seven lamps of fire before the throne, "the seven spirits of God," which many Christian readers take as the Holy Spirit in fullness.

a: make them by their pattern, the one you are being shown on the mountain
t: A copy of something in heaven
p: Hebrews 8:5 quotes this verse: the earthly tent copies a heavenly one.
b: Moses is shown a tavnit, a model or plan (also 25:9; 26:30). Other ancient builders claimed the same. King Gudea of Lagash (about 2100 BC) wrote that a god showed him the plan of his temple in a dream. Later Jewish and Christian writers took this to mean that a sanctuary exists in heaven and the tabernacle copies it (Wisdom of Solomon 9:8; Revelation 11:19; 15:5). Hebrews quotes this verse to argue that the earthly priests serve "an outline and a shadow of the things in heaven," while Christ serves in the true tent (Hebrews 8:2–5; 9:23–24). Philo read it the way Plato would: Moses saw the unseen ideas of which the tent is an image. Stephen also cites it (Acts 7:44).

a: with cherubim worked into them
p: Inside, the priests saw cherubim all around them, as if standing in the guarded garden or in heaven.
b: The inner curtains formed the ceiling and walls of the tabernacle, so a priest inside saw woven cherubim above and around him. Cherubim guarded the way back into Eden (Genesis 3:24), and the entrance of the tabernacle, like Eden's, faced east (27:13; Genesis 3:24). Many scholars, Jewish and Christian, have read the tabernacle as a return to the garden: gold and onyx (Genesis 2:11–12; Exodus 25:7), a tree-shaped lampstand, and cherubim guarding the place where God walks with people. Gordon Wenham calls Eden itself "an archetypal sanctuary."

a: So the tabernacle will be one.
p: Fifty gold clasps join two great panels into one dwelling. The word for 'one' returns in 26:11.
b: Each set of five curtains made a panel about 42 by 30 feet (28 by 20 cubits). The fifty gold clasps join the two panels so that "the tabernacle will be one" (echad), and the goat-hair tent is made "one" the same way (26:11). Some Jewish interpreters heard an echo of "the LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4), and Christian readers have heard the unity of the body made of many members (1 Corinthians 12:12). The plain sense is practical: two large panels could be carried separately and joined on site.

a: Make curtains of goat hair for a tent over the tabernacle.
p: Black goat-hair cloth is still the material of Bedouin tents. It sheds rain and lets air through.
b: Goat-hair cloth, usually black, is the traditional fabric of desert tents, still used by Bedouin today. It swells when wet and keeps out rain. Over the bright linen curtains, then, stood a plain dark tent, and over that two layers of leather (26:14). From outside the tabernacle looked like an ordinary nomad's tent, only larger. Song of Songs 1:5 compares a dark beauty to "the tents of Kedar," the black tents of an Arabian tribe. Michael Homan has compared the whole structure with the royal war tent of Pharaoh Ramesses II in his camp at Kadesh, about 1274 BC, which also had a two-to-one plan with the throne room at the back.

a: For the tabernacle make frames of acacia wood that stand upright.
p: Qerashim were once pictured as solid planks. Many now think they were open frames.
b: The KJV calls the qerashim "boards," and older pictures show solid planks forming wooden walls. But planks 15 feet tall and over 2 feet wide (10 by 1.5 cubits) would be very heavy, and the woven cherubim on the inner curtains could not be seen behind a solid wall. So many scholars, following A. R. S. Kennedy, think they were open frames, two uprights joined by crossbars, with the "two pegs" (26:17) at the bottom fitting into silver bases. The Hebrew allows either. Ezekiel 27:6 uses the same word for the deck of a ship.

a: make forty silver bases
p: The bases were cast from the half-shekel paid by every counted man. The tent stood on their ransom money.
b: Each frame stood in two sockets of silver. Exodus 38:25–27 says that this silver came from the half shekel each man paid when the people were counted, the "atonement money" of 30:11–16, and that one talent of silver went into each base. So the whole dwelling of God literally rested on the ransom paid for every Israelite, rich and poor alike (30:15). There were a hundred silver bases in all: forty on each long side, sixteen at the back, and four for the veil.

a: the way it was planned, as you have been shown on the mountain
p: Was the tabernacle a real tent in the desert, or a priestly picture of the temple drawn back into the past?
b: Traditional Jewish and Christian readers take the tabernacle as a real structure built at Sinai. Kenneth Kitchen and James Hoffmeier point to Egyptian portable shrines and frame buildings, and Daniel Fleming to a large public tent used in worship at Mari about 1800 BC, evidence that tent sanctuaries were old among West Semitic peoples. Julius Wellhausen argued in 1878 that the tabernacle was Solomon's temple folded up and carried back into the desert by priestly writers (P). Menahem Haran agreed that it mirrors the Jerusalem temple, but with Yehezkel Kaufmann, Jacob Milgrom and Israel Knohl he dated P before the exile, and Avi Hurvitz found its Hebrew older than Ezekiel's. Frank Moore Cross linked the tent with David's tent for the ark (2 Samuel 6:17), and Richard Friedman suggested it once stood inside Solomon's temple. The text presents it as a plan shown on the mountain.

a: Make a veil
p: The parokhet divided the holiest room. The Gospels say the temple veil tore when Jesus died.
b: The parokhet, a heavy woven curtain, closed off the most holy place. Only the high priest passed through it, once a year, with blood (Leviticus 16:2, 12–15). Matthew, Mark and Luke all report that when Jesus died, "the sanctuary curtain was torn in two from the top down to the bottom" (Mark 15:38). Hebrews reads the veil as a picture of Christ's own body, through which believers now enter God's presence (Hebrews 10:19–20; 6:19–20). Jewish tradition keeps the word: the curtain in front of the Torah ark in a synagogue is called a parokhet.
r: Leviticus 16:2; Leviticus 16:12–15; Mark 15:38; Matthew 27:51; Luke 23:45; Hebrews 6:19–20; Hebrews 9:3; Hebrews 10:19–20

a: between the holy place and the most holy place
p: 'Holy of holies' is a Hebrew way to say 'the holiest.' The inner room was a perfect cube.
b: Hebrew makes a superlative by repeating a noun: "holy of the holies" means "the most holy," as "song of songs" means "the finest song." The inner room was 10 by 10 by 10 cubits, a perfect cube, half the size of the outer room. Solomon's inner room was also a cube, 20 cubits each way (1 Kings 6:20), and the new Jerusalem of Revelation is a cube too (Revelation 21:16), which many read as saying that the whole city has become the most holy place.

a: Set the table outside the veil
p: The incense altar belongs here, but it is not described until 30:1–10. Two ancient texts move it here.
b: The rooms are furnished here with the ark, table and lampstand, but the gold altar of incense, which stood in front of the veil (30:6; 40:5), is not mentioned until chapter 30. Many critical scholars since Wellhausen have taken 30:1–10 as a later addition. Others answer that chapters 25–29 describe how God will meet Israel, and chapter 30 moves on to the people's response: incense, ransom and washing. Two ancient witnesses, the Samaritan Pentateuch and a Dead Sea scroll, solve the puzzle by placing 30:1–10 right after this verse; see the variant on this verse.

a: Build the altar of acacia wood.
p: A wooden box covered with bronze, about 7½ feet square and 4½ feet high, hollow inside.
b: The altar of burnt offering stood in the courtyard in front of the tent. It was about 7½ feet square and 4½ feet high, a hollow wooden frame covered with bronze (27:8). A wooden altar would burn, so many interpreters think it was filled with earth or stones when the camp stopped, in line with the rule that an altar be made of earth or uncut stone (20:24–25). Others suggest the bronze grate (27:4) held the fire above the wood. The text does not explain. Solomon's bronze altar was much larger (2 Chronicles 4:1).

a: Make horns for it at its four corners
p: Horned altars have been dug up in Israel. Grabbing the horns was a plea for safety.
b: Stone altars with knob-like horns at the corners have been excavated in Israel, the best known from Beersheba, Megiddo and Tel Dan. In the Bible blood was put on the horns (29:12; Leviticus 4:7), and a man in danger could grab them to claim protection, as Adonijah and Joab did (1 Kings 1:50; 2:28). Amos 3:14 warns that the horns of the altar at Bethel will be cut off. Horns stood for strength, so the horns may mark the altar's most powerful point. Revelation 9:13 hears a voice from "the four horns of the golden altar before God."
r: 29:12; 30:10; Leviticus 4:7; 1 Kings 1:50; 1 Kings 2:28; Amos 3:14; Psalm 118:27; Revelation 9:13

a: Make the courtyard of the tabernacle.
p: About 150 by 75 feet, with linen walls 7½ feet high, open to the sky.
b: The courtyard was 100 by 50 cubits, about 150 by 75 feet, roughly a fifth to a quarter of an American football field. Its walls were linen hangings about 7½ feet high (27:18), so a person outside could not see in, but the tent itself, 10 cubits high, rose above them. The plan is two squares side by side. The eastern square held the altar and basin. The tent stood in the western square, and on a common reconstruction the ark, in the most holy place, sat at the center of that square. Everything in the camp faced east, toward the gate (Numbers 2).

a: pure oil pressed from olives for the light
p: Katit means oil from olives crushed by hand, the purest first oil, which burns with little smoke.
b: Katit, "crushed" or "beaten," means oil from olives pounded in a mortar rather than pressed with heavy weights. Only the first, clearest drops were used, which burn bright and with little smoke. The Mishnah (Menachot 8:4–5) explains that the first drops went to the lampstand and the rest could be used for grain offerings. The daily lamp needs a daily gift from the people: the lamp is the priests' work, but the oil is Israel's. Leviticus 24:1–4 repeats this command almost word for word.
orig: שֶׁמֶן זַיִת זָךְ כָּתִית (shemen zayit zakh katit)

a: a lamp can be lit to burn always
p: Tamid here means 'regularly,' every night, not burning day and night without a break.
b: Ner tamid is often translated "a perpetual lamp," and synagogues keep a ner tamid burning before the Torah ark at all times. But the next verse says the lamp burns "from evening until morning," and 1 Samuel 3:3 mentions that "God's lamp was not yet out" before dawn. So tamid here means "regularly, every night," as the daily offering is the tamid offering (29:42). The synagogue custom is a later, beautiful extension of this command.

a: in the tent of meeting
p: This is the first use of the name in Exodus. In 33:7 the same name is used for a different tent.
b: Ohel mo'ed appears here for the first time, and well over a hundred times in the Torah. The tent is where God "meets" with Moses and the people by appointment (25:22; 29:42–43). In 33:7–11 the same name is given to a small tent pitched outside the camp, where Moses spoke with God before the tabernacle was built. Critical scholars see two traditions: an older oracle tent outside the camp, and the priestly tabernacle in the middle of the camp. Traditional readers see a temporary tent used until the tabernacle was ready.

a: Aaron and his sons
p: Aaron's priesthood is mentioned before it is created in chapter 28. The outline moves from God to people.
b: Before chapter 28 has named the priests, Aaron and his sons are already assigned the lamp. The order of the instructions moves outward from the ark (25:10) to the furnishings, tent, altar and court, and then to the people who serve there. Aaron, Moses' brother, has been his spokesman since 4:14–16 and stood beside him through the plagues. Here his role changes from speaker to priest. He will soon also be the one who makes the calf (32:1–6, 21–24), a tension the book does not hide.

a: to be my priests
p: Jews still honor Aaron's descendants as kohanim. Hebrews contrasts his priesthood with Christ's.
b: From here on, only Aaron and his sons may serve at the altar (Numbers 3:10; 18:1–7). In Jewish life the kohanim, men who trace their family to Aaron, still give the priestly blessing in synagogue (Numbers 6:24–26). The New Testament letter to the Hebrews says Aaron's priesthood was real but temporary: Christ is a priest "in the line of Melchizedek," not Aaron (Hebrews 5:1–6; 7:11–28), and 1 Peter 2:9 calls the whole church "a royal priesthood," echoing "a kingdom of priests" (19:6). Many critical scholars think the priestly writers stressed Aaron's line because, in their own time, the Jerusalem priests claimed descent from him, and that other priestly families once had rival claims (compare 32:26–29).
r: Numbers 3:10; Numbers 6:24–26; Numbers 18:1–7; Leviticus 10:1–2; Hebrews 5:1–6; Hebrews 7:11–28; 1 Peter 2:9; 19:6

a: for glory and for beauty
p: Kavod and tif'eret: the same words describe God's own glory. The clothes make the office visible.
b: Kavod is the word for God's "glory" that fills the tabernacle at the end of the book (40:34), and tif'eret means splendor or beauty. The priest is dressed to reflect, in a small way, the glory of the one he serves. The Bible's story of clothing began when God made garments for Adam and Eve (Genesis 3:21). Here God designs clothes again, this time for coming near. Zechariah 3:3–5 pictures the high priest Joshua in filthy clothes being re-dressed in clean ones, a picture of forgiveness.

a: whom I have filled with a spirit of wisdom
p: Chokhmah here is the skill of a craftsman, a gift from God's Spirit.
b: In English "wisdom" sounds like book learning or good judgment. The Hebrew chokhmah often means practical skill, the know-how of a weaver, goldsmith or sailor (Psalm 107:27 says sailors' "wisdom" was swallowed up). The "skilled" people here are literally "wise of heart." Exodus says such skill is a gift of God's spirit, the same claim it makes for Bezalel (31:3; 35:31). The Bible here honors craftsmanship as holy work.

a: These are the clothes they will make
p: The Talmud says each garment atoned for a different sin. Christians read the high priest as a picture of Christ.
b: The high priest wore eight garments, the ordinary priests four (28:40–42). The Talmud (Zevachim 88b; Arakhin 16a) says each garment atoned for a sin: the tunic for bloodshed, the linen shorts for sexual sin, the turban for pride, the sash for the thoughts of the heart, the breastpiece for corrupt judgment, the ephod for idolatry, the robe for evil speech, and the gold plate for brazen faces. After the temple fell, the rabbis taught that prayer, study and good deeds take the place of sacrifice and priestly clothes. Christian writers from Origen and Bede on read the robes as pictures of Christ's virtues, and Hebrews calls Jesus the "great high priest" (Hebrews 4:14).

a: They will make the ephod
p: An ephod was a wrap or apron. Other ephods in the Bible were used to ask God questions, and one became an idol.
b: The ephod seems to have been an apron or wrap held up by shoulder straps and tied with a woven band. Priests and boys serving at the shrine wore simple linen ephods (1 Samuel 2:18; 22:18), and David danced before the ark in one (2 Samuel 6:14). An ephod was also used to ask God for guidance (1 Samuel 23:9–12; 30:7–8), probably because the Urim and Thummim were kept with it (28:30). Gideon made a gold ephod that became an object of worship (Judges 8:27), and Micah made one for his household shrine (Judges 17:5). The high priest's ephod was the most splendid of all.
r: 1 Samuel 2:18; 1 Samuel 23:9–12; 1 Samuel 30:7–8; 2 Samuel 6:14; Judges 8:27; Judges 17:5; Hosea 3:4

a: Aaron will carry their names before the LORD on his two shoulders
p: The priest carries Israel on his shoulders and over his heart (28:29) whenever he goes before God.
b: Twelve names are carried twice: on the shoulders, the place of bearing burdens, and over the heart on the breastpiece (28:29). When the priest enters God's presence, the whole people goes in with him, "to bring them to mind" before God. The pattern of carrying on the shoulder returns in Isaiah 9:6 ("the rule is on his shoulder") and in Jesus' parable of the shepherd who finds his lost sheep and lays it on his shoulders (Luke 15:5). Hebrews 7:25 says Christ "always lives to intercede" for his people.

a: Make a breastpiece for decisions
p: It was a pouch, folded double. It held the Urim and Thummim, the means of hearing God's decision.
b: The choshen mishpat was not armor, though the KJV calls it a "breastplate." It was a square of woven cloth folded double into a pouch about 9 inches square (28:16). Mishpat means "judgment" or "decision." It is called the breastpiece "of judgment" because it held the Urim and Thummim, through which God's decisions were sought (28:30; Numbers 27:21). The Septuagint calls it the logeion, "the oracle." The Plain English says "for decisions" to show what it was for.

a: carnelian, topaz and emerald
t: Twelve stones nobody can name for sure
p: Ancient gem names do not match modern ones. Every English Bible guesses differently.
b: The twelve Hebrew names (28:17–20) are hard to identify. Ancient names often went by color, and the Septuagint, Josephus (who gives two lists, War 5.234 and Antiquities 3.168) and the rabbis disagree. The Plain choices, with how sure they are: odem carnelian (likely); pitdah topaz (likely; Greek topazion, probably peridot); bareqet emerald (guess); nofekh turquoise (guess); sappir lapis lazuli (likely); yahalom quartz (guess: from "strike," a hard stone; not diamond, which could not be engraved); leshem jacinth, shevo agate, achlamah amethyst (guesses following the Greek); tarshish chrysolite (guess); shoham onyx (likely); yashpeh jasper (likely). The Greek row two ends with iaspis, jasper, and puts onychion at yashpeh, so the two lists are offset. Eight of Revelation's twelve foundation stones (21:19–20) match the Greek list.

a: over his heart
p: The names are worn over the heart, the seat of thought and love in Hebrew.
b: In Hebrew the heart is the place of thinking, deciding and loving. So the priest carries the tribes not just on his body but in his mind and care. The bride in Song of Songs asks, "Put me like a seal on your heart" (Song of Songs 8:6), and the names here are engraved "like a seal" (28:21). Christian readers have often heard in this verse a picture of Christ, who carries his people's names before the Father. The phrase "over his heart" appears three times in two verses (28:29–30).

a: the Urim and the Thummim
p: Probably sacred lots for asking God yes-or-no questions. The words may mean 'lights and perfections.'
b: Exodus never explains what the Urim and Thummim were or how they worked. It simply assumes them. Most scholars think they were lots, objects drawn or cast to get a yes or no answer from God. The longer Greek text of 1 Samuel 14:41 has Saul pray, "If the guilt is in me, give Urim; if it is in your people, give Thummim." The words may mean "lights and perfections" (or, from arar, "curses," and tam, "innocent"). They begin with the first and last letters of the Hebrew alphabet, alef and tav. The Septuagint translated them "the revealing and the truth." Yale University's seal still carries the Hebrew words.
r: Leviticus 8:8; Numbers 27:21; Deuteronomy 33:8; 1 Samuel 14:41; 1 Samuel 28:6; Ezra 2:63; Nehemiah 7:65

a: carry the decisions for the Israelites over his heart
p: Josephus and the Talmud said the stones lit up. Scholars think of lots. The practice ended early.
b: Josephus, writing about AD 94, said the stones on the high priest's shoulders and breastpiece shone with light to give God's answer, but that this had stopped two hundred years before his time (Jewish Antiquities 3.214–218). The Talmud (Yoma 73a–b) says the letters of the tribal names on the stones lit up or stood out to spell the answer, and that only a priest filled with the Spirit could read them. Most modern scholars think instead of two lots kept in the pouch. Either way, after David's time the Bible no longer reports their use, and by the return from exile no priest had them (Ezra 2:63). Joseph Smith later used the name for the seer stones he said he used to translate the Book of Mormon.

a: Make the robe that goes under the ephod all of violet.
p: The robe was solid blue, the color of the tassels every Israelite wore and the cloth that covered the ark.
b: The robe worn under the ephod was all tekhelet, the costly blue-violet dye from sea snails (see the note on 25:4). Blue covered the ark when it was carried (Numbers 4:6) and was the color of the thread in every Israelite's tassels, by which "you will see it and remember all the LORD's commands" (Numbers 15:38–39). The rabbis said blue is like the sea, the sea like the sky, and the sky like the throne of glory (Talmud, Menachot 43b). It was woven in one piece with a strong edge around the neck so it would not tear (28:32). The high priest was forbidden to tear his clothes in mourning (Leviticus 21:10).

a: so he will not die
p: The bells announce the priest. The popular story of a rope tied to his ankle is not in the Bible.
b: Why must the priest be heard? Ramban compared a person who enters a king's room, who should not burst in unannounced. Others think the sound marked the priest as rightly dressed and authorized, and many modern scholars think bells were believed to keep evil away from a holy threshold. A popular story says the high priest had a rope tied to his ankle so that, if he died in the most holy place, others could pull him out. The Bible and the Talmud say nothing of this. It is a late legend, usually traced to the medieval Zohar, and even that source is disputed.

a: 'Holy to the LORD.'
p: The words on the priest's forehead will one day be written on bells and cooking pots (Zechariah 14:20).
b: The gold plate (tsits, perhaps "flower") on Aaron's forehead declares that he belongs wholly to God. Zechariah looks forward to a day when even the bells of horses and the cooking pots of Jerusalem will be engraved "Holy to the LORD" (Zechariah 14:20–21): the holiness of the high priest will spread to all of ordinary life. Revelation pictures God's servants with his name on their foreheads (Revelation 14:1; 22:4), and Christians often connect the plate with the call to be "a holy priesthood" (1 Peter 2:5).

a: Aaron will carry the guilt
p: Nasa avon, 'lift guilt,' can mean bear punishment or carry it away. The priest does both.
b: "Carry guilt" (nasa avon) has two senses in the Bible. A guilty person "carries his guilt" when he suffers its punishment (28:43; Leviticus 5:1). God "carries guilt" when he forgives it, lifting it away (34:7, "forgiving guilt" is the same phrase). Here the high priest carries the guilt attached to the people's gifts, any fault in how they were offered, so that the gifts are still accepted. The scapegoat "carries" Israel's guilt into the desert (Leviticus 16:22), and the servant of Isaiah 53 "carries" the sins of many (Isaiah 53:11–12). Christian readers connect this with Christ, who "carried the sins of many" (Hebrews 9:28; 1 Peter 2:24).

a: fill their hands
p: The Hebrew idiom for ordaining a priest is 'to fill his hand.'
b: "Fill their hands" translates the idiom mille' yad, "fill the hand." It is used for installing a priest (29:9; Judges 17:5, 12; 1 Kings 13:33). Its origin is debated. It may come from placing the first offerings in the new priest's hands (29:24), or from paying him his first share. The ram of ordination is called the ram of millu'im, "filling" (29:22). The same idiom returns in a startling way when Moses tells the Levites to "fill your hands" after the calf (32:29).

a: Make linen undershorts for them to cover their naked bodies.
p: Some ancient priests served naked. Israel's priests had to be covered.
b: In ancient Sumer some priests performed rituals naked, as the Warka vase and other carvings show. Israel's law insists on modesty before God: the altar is not to have steps that expose the priest (20:26), and here linen undershorts are required. The Hebrew "flesh of nakedness" is a polite expression. Ezekiel's vision adds that priests must wear linen, not wool, so that they will not sweat (Ezekiel 44:17–18). The ordinary priests' clothes were simple white linen, the dress also worn by angels in visions (Daniel 10:5; Revelation 15:6).

a: Here is what you will do to them to set them apart as my priests.
p: This chapter gives the plan. Leviticus 8–9 tells how Moses carried it out, step by step.
b: The ordination rite is commanded here and performed in Leviticus 8, where nearly every step is repeated, ending each time "as the LORD commanded Moses." On the eighth day Aaron offers his first sacrifices and fire comes out from the LORD (Leviticus 9:1, 23–24). The pattern of command and fulfillment is the same as in the building chapters (35–40). Washing, dressing and anointing were also part of installing kings and priests in other ancient cultures. Christian writers have compared the washing of 29:4 with baptism (Hebrews 10:22).

a: Take the anointing oil, pour it on his head, and anoint him.
p: Pouring oil on the head marked a person as chosen for God's service. 'Messiah' means 'anointed one.'
b: Only Aaron has the oil poured on his head (also Leviticus 8:12). Psalm 133:2 remembers it as "precious oil on the head, running down on the beard, Aaron's beard, down to the collar of his robes." Kings were later anointed in the same way (1 Samuel 10:1; 16:13), and some prophets too (1 Kings 19:16). The high priest is called "the anointed priest" (Leviticus 4:3). The Hebrew mashiach, "anointed," gives the word "Messiah," and its Greek equivalent christos gives "Christ." For the recipe of the oil, see 30:22–33.
r: 30:22–33; Leviticus 4:3; Leviticus 8:12; Psalm 133:2; 1 Samuel 10:1; 1 Samuel 16:13; Luke 4:18; Acts 10:38

a: Aaron and his sons are to lay their hands on the bull's head.
t: Why lay hands on the animal?
p: Some read it as transfer of sin to the animal. Others read it as 'this animal is mine, offered for me.'
b: The person offering leans his hands on the animal's head before it is killed (Leviticus 1:4; 3:2; 4:4). On the Day of Atonement the high priest lays both hands on the scapegoat and confesses Israel's sins over it (Leviticus 16:21), which suggests a transfer of sin. Many Christian interpreters read every laying on of hands this way, as a picture of substitution. Jacob Milgrom and others argue that in most sacrifices one hand is laid on, and it marks ownership: this animal is offered by me and for me. The rabbis required the offerer to lean with all his strength (Talmud, Chagigah 16b).
r: Leviticus 1:4; Leviticus 3:2; Leviticus 4:4; Leviticus 16:21; Numbers 8:12; Isaiah 53:6

a: But burn the bull's meat, its hide and its dung in a fire outside the camp.
p: Hebrews 13:11–13 links this rule to Jesus, who suffered outside the city gate.
b: The chatat, often called "sin offering" and by many scholars "purification offering," cleanses the altar and the people (29:36). When the blood is used for the priests themselves, the meat may not be eaten by them and is burned outside the camp (Leviticus 4:11–12; 6:30). Hebrews uses this rule: the bodies of those animals are burned outside the camp, and so Jesus suffered outside the city gate; it calls believers to go out to him, outside the camp (Hebrews 13:11–13). Compare Moses' tent "outside the camp" in 33:7.

a: a soothing smell
p: Reach nichoach is literally 'a smell of rest.' It first appears after Noah's flood.
b: Reach nichoach means "a calming smell" or "a smell of rest" (nuach, "rest"). It first appears in Genesis 8:21, when the LORD smells Noah's offering and promises never again to curse the ground. The word nichoach sounds like Noah's name. The phrase does not mean that God gets hungry. It is a picture of God accepting the offering and being at peace with the giver. Paul uses it of Christ, who gave himself "as an offering and a sacrifice to God, a soothing smell" (Ephesians 5:2), and of the gifts of the church (Philippians 4:18).

a: Put it on the lobe of Aaron's right ear
p: Blood on the ear, hand and foot: the whole person is set apart, to listen, to act and to walk with God.
b: The blood touches the extremities of the right side of the body. Many interpreters, Jewish and Christian, read this as covering the whole person: the ear that hears God, the hand that serves him, the foot that walks in his ways. The same three points are touched with blood and oil when a person healed of a skin disease is restored to the community (Leviticus 14:14, 17). Some scholars think the extremities were thought to be where impurity could enter, so they were sealed by the blood. The right side was the side of strength and honor.

a: wave them before the LORD as a wave offering
p: Tenufah was long pictured as a swinging motion. Many now think it means lifting the gift toward God.
b: Tenufah is traditionally "wave offering," and the rabbis described the priest moving it back and forth and up and down (Talmud, Menachot 62a). Jacob Milgrom argued from Egyptian pictures that it was a raising or presenting gesture, lifting the gift to hand it over to God, who then gives it back to the priest as his share (29:26–28). The same root is used in 35:22 for the gold the people "waved" to the LORD, where it simply means "dedicated." The Hebrew says "you will wave them": Moses does the waving, with the gifts resting in the priests' palms, as he does in Leviticus 8:27. Rashi says that Moses and the priests held the gifts together, Moses' hands beneath theirs. The Plain English keeps the traditional term "wave offering."

a: their peace offerings
p: Shelamim were shared meals: part for God, part for the priest, most for the worshiper's family.
b: The shelamim, from the root of shalom, are offerings of well-being or fellowship. Unlike the burnt offering, which was all burned, most of the meat was eaten by the worshiper and his family in a festive meal. The fat went on the altar for God, and the breast and right thigh went to the priests (Leviticus 7:11–34). The rule here sets up that share for all time. Some translations call them "fellowship offerings" or "offerings of well-being." They are the sacrifice of joy, offered at thanksgivings and vows.

a: No outsider may eat them
p: Zar here means a non-priest, any Israelite outside the priestly family.
b: Zar is often translated "stranger" (KJV) and can mean foreigner. Here it means anyone outside the priestly family, including ordinary Israelites (Numbers 3:10; 16:40). The same word describes the "strange" incense of 30:9 and the "strange fire" of Nadab and Abihu (Leviticus 10:1): something not authorized for that holy use. The point is not ethnic exclusion but the boundary of holiness around the altar.

a: Cleanse the altar from sin when you make atonement for it
p: Kipper here is done to an object. It means to wipe clean and purify, not only to forgive.
b: Altars do not sin, yet the priest must "make atonement" (kipper) for this one. This shows that kipper means more than "forgive." It means to purge or wipe clean something polluted by the people's sins and impurities, so that God can stay among them. Jacob Milgrom compared the sanctuary to a picture of Dorian Gray: Israel's sins left stains on God's house, and the blood of the chatat washed them off. Many scholars link kipper to an Akkadian verb meaning "wipe off." Others prefer "cover" or "ransom" (compare 30:12).

a: Anything that touches the altar will become holy.
p: Does the altar make things holy by touch, or must whoever touches it be holy? Both readings are argued.
b: The Hebrew kol hannogea' bammizbeach yiqdash can mean "whatever touches the altar becomes holy" (holiness is passed on like a charge, so the object now belongs to God) or "whoever touches the altar must be holy" (only consecrated priests may touch it). Haggai 2:11–13 shows that, by his time, holiness was not thought to pass on by indirect touch, while impurity was. Jacob Milgrom discussed at length whether people, or only objects, were thought to be affected. In the Gospels the pattern is reversed: Jesus touches the unclean and they become clean (Mark 1:41; 5:27–29).

a: two yearling lambs, every day, without fail
p: The tamid, morning and evening, shaped Jewish prayer times. Its end in AD 70 was mourned.
b: The tamid, the regular daily offering, was the heartbeat of the temple. The morning and afternoon prayers of Judaism (Shacharit and Minchah) took their times from it (Talmud, Berakhot 26b), and the Mishnah's tractate Tamid describes the service in the Second Temple. Daniel speaks of a king who will "do away with the regular offering" (Daniel 11:31; Daniel 8:11), and the Mishnah lists the day the tamid stopped during the Roman siege among Israel's great disasters (Taanit 4:6). In Acts 3:1 Peter and John go up to the temple "at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour," the time of the evening offering.
r: Numbers 28:3–8; Daniel 8:11; Daniel 11:31; Psalm 141:2; Acts 3:1; Hebrews 10:11

a: at dusk
p: The Hebrew says 'between the evenings,' probably from sunset to dark, or afternoon to sunset.
b: The phrase bein ha'arbayim, "between the two evenings," also sets the time of the Passover lamb (12:6) and the lighting of the lamps (30:8). The Samaritans and some Jewish groups took it to mean the time between sunset and full dark. The Pharisees and later rabbis took it as the afternoon, from when the sun begins to decline until sunset, and in Jesus' day the evening offering was made at about 3 p.m. (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 14.65). "Twilight" is the usual modern rendering.

a: There I will meet with you, to speak to you there.
p: The chapter ends with God's reason for everything: to meet, to speak, and to live among his people.
b: The rites of the chapter build to a promise in three steps: God will meet with Israel (29:42–43), make the place holy by his glory (29:43–44), and live among them as their God (29:45–46). The last verse states the purpose of the exodus itself: God brought Israel out of Egypt "to live in their midst." The covenant formula "I will be their God" runs from Genesis 17:7 through the prophets (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 37:27) to the last chapters of the Bible (Revelation 21:3).

a: Make an altar for burning incense.
p: Two stone incense altars from the shrine at Arad still held traces of burned frankincense.
b: Small horned altars for incense have been found at many sites in Israel, including Megiddo and Tel Miqne (Ekron). At the Judahite fortress of Arad (700s BC), two limestone altars stood at the entrance to a shrine's inner room, much as the gold altar stood before the veil. A 2020 study by Eran Arie, Baruch Rosen and Dvory Namdar found residue of frankincense on the larger altar and of cannabis on the smaller one. The tabernacle altar was small, about 18 inches square and 3 feet high, made of acacia wood covered with gold. For why it appears here rather than in chapter 25, see the note on 26:35.

a: Place the altar in front of the veil
p: Exodus puts the incense altar outside the veil. Hebrews seems to put it inside. Readers have long debated why.
b: Exodus clearly places the gold altar in the outer room, in front of the veil (also 40:26). Hebrews 9:3–4 describes the most holy place as "having a golden thymiatērion and the ark." Some take the Greek word to mean a golden censer, the fire pan the high priest carried into the inner room on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:12–13). Others think Hebrews means the altar "belonged to" the inner room in function, since it stood right against the veil and its incense filled the holiest place, as 1 Kings 6:22 says the altar "belonged to the inner room." Some critical scholars think the author of Hebrews simply placed it differently.

a: It is to be incense burned before the LORD without fail
p: The incense rose at the hours of prayer. Psalms and Revelation link it with the prayers of God's people.
b: Incense was burned every morning and evening, at the times of the daily offering (29:38–42). "Let my prayer be set up as incense in front of you" (Psalm 141:2). Luke tells that Zechariah was burning incense in the temple while "all the people were outside praying at the time of the incense," when the angel appeared to him (Luke 1:8–11). In Revelation the elders hold golden bowls of incense, "which are the prayers of the saints," and an angel offers incense with their prayers on the golden altar before the throne (Revelation 5:8; 8:3–4).

a: you must not offer any strange incense
p: Zarah means foreign or not authorized. Aaron's sons died for offering 'strange fire' (Leviticus 10:1).
b: The incense is called zarah, "strange" or "foreign," meaning any mixture other than the one commanded (30:34–38) or offered at the wrong time. The same word appears in the death of Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu, who offered "strange fire, which he had not commanded them" (Leviticus 10:1). Many modern versions say "unauthorized." King Uzziah was struck with a skin disease for burning incense himself (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). The altar is reserved for one purpose only: no animal or grain offerings, no drink offerings.

a: Once a year Aaron will make atonement on its horns.
p: The first hint of Yom Kippur in the Bible. Leviticus 16 gives the full rite.
b: This is the first mention of the yearly day when the high priest purifies the altars with blood. Leviticus 16 describes it in full: the high priest goes behind the veil with incense and blood, sprinkles the atonement lid, then purifies "the altar that is before the LORD" by putting blood on its horns (Leviticus 16:18–19), and sends a goat into the wilderness. The day falls on the tenth of the seventh month (Leviticus 16:29), Yom Kippur. Jewish tradition also ties this day to the golden calf: Moses came down with the second tablets on Yom Kippur (see the note on 34:29).

a: so that no plague will strike them as you enroll them
p: David's census brought a plague (2 Samuel 24). Readers have offered several reasons.
b: Counting people was risky in the ancient world, and David's census ended in a plague (2 Samuel 24:1–17). Why? Some say a census was for military service and taxes, so it showed trust in numbers rather than God. Others say counting claims ownership, and the people belong to God, so each must pay a ransom (kofer) for himself. E. A. Speiser argued that texts from Mari link a troop census with a rite of purification, though his reading of the key word tebibtum has since been questioned. The rabbis drew a practical rule: Israel should not be counted by heads but by objects, such as coins (Rashi on this verse; Talmud, Yoma 22b). This is why Jewish custom counts a prayer group with a verse of ten words instead of numbers.

a: half a shekel, by the holy place's shekel
p: A shekel was a weight of silver, about 2/5 ounce. The tax became the temple tax of Jesus' day.
b: Coins did not exist until about 600 BC. A shekel was a weight, about 11.5 grams (2/5 ounce) of silver, and a gerah was a twentieth of it. "The holy place's shekel" was the standard kept at the shrine. In Nehemiah's day the people pledged a third of a shekel a year (Nehemiah 10:32). By the first century every Jewish man, even outside the land, paid a yearly half shekel to the temple (Mishnah, Shekalim), and Jesus had Peter pay it with a coin from a fish's mouth (Matthew 17:24–27). Jews still give a symbolic "half shekel" to charity before Purim.

a: The rich are not to pay more than half a shekel, and the poor are not to pay less
p: Every life is ransomed at the same price. The rabbis heard a lesson of equality and unity.
b: Freewill gifts depended on what each person had (25:2; 35:5), but the ransom for a life was fixed. Every Israelite counted exactly the same before God, and the silver went into the bases on which the tabernacle stood (38:25–27). Jewish teachers have also noted that it is a half shekel: no one is whole alone, and only together do the people form a whole. Christian readers have compared the equal ransom with 1 Peter 1:18–19: that believers were bought free "not with things that perish, silver or gold, but with the costly blood of Christ."

a: make a basin of bronze with a bronze stand
p: Priests had to wash hands and feet before serving. Solomon's temple had a huge bronze 'sea.'
b: The basin stood between the altar and the tent, so priests washed before every approach to God (30:20). It was made from the women's bronze mirrors (38:8). Solomon's temple had a vast bronze basin called "the sea" and ten smaller ones (1 Kings 7:23–39). Psalm 24:3–4 asks, "Who can climb the LORD's mountain?" and answers, "Someone whose hands are clean and whose heart is pure." Christian writers have linked the basin with baptism and the washing of rebirth (Titus 3:5; Hebrews 10:22), and some with Jesus washing his disciples' feet (John 13:8–10). The "sea of glass" before God's throne in Revelation 4:6 may echo the temple's sea.
r: 38:8; 40:30–32; 1 Kings 7:23–39; Psalm 24:3–4; Psalm 26:6; John 13:8–10; Titus 3:5; Hebrews 10:22; Revelation 4:6

a: Take the finest spices
p: Myrrh came from Arabia and East Africa; cinnamon and cassia from as far as South Asia.
b: Myrrh is a resin from trees in southern Arabia and Somalia. Cinnamon and cassia are tree barks native to South and Southeast Asia, and reached the Near East through long trade routes. "Sweet cane" (qeneh bosem) is probably calamus or lemongrass. A claim made in 1936 by the scholar Sula Benet, and repeated widely online, says it was cannabis, but most scholars reject this. Five hundred shekels is about 12½ pounds (5.7 kg), and a hin is about a gallon (3.7 liters), so the oil was a large, very fragrant batch. Psalm 45:8 describes a king's robes fragrant "with myrrh, aloes and cassia."
r: Genesis 37:25; 1 Kings 10:10; Psalm 45:8; Song of Songs 4:14; Revelation 18:13

a: will be cut off from his people
p: Karet may mean exile, early death at God's hand, or the end of one's family line. Readers differ.
b: The penalty karet, "cutting off," is threatened for a number of sins (12:15; 30:38; 31:14; Leviticus 17:4). The rabbis understood it as a punishment carried out by God, not a human court: early death or dying without children (Talmud, Moed Katan 28a; Mishnah, Keritot 1:1). Others think it means being expelled from the community. Jacob Milgrom argued that it means the end of a person's family line and perhaps of his life beyond death. In 31:14 it stands next to the death penalty, which suggests the two are different.

a: stacte, onycha and galbanum
p: Stacte, onycha, galbanum and frankincense. The rabbis later listed eleven spices.
b: Nataf ("drop," Greek stactē) is a resin, perhaps from storax or balsam trees. Shechelet (onycha, "fingernail") is probably the shell lid of a sea snail, which gives off a strong smell when burned. Chelbenah is galbanum, a gum with a sharp, bitter smell. Levonah is frankincense, the "white" resin of Arabian trees. The Talmud (Keritot 6a–b) lists eleven spices in the temple incense, recited daily in many prayer books as Pittum ha-Ketoret, and draws a lesson from galbanum: a bad-smelling spice in the holy mix teaches that sinners belong in the community's prayer too.

a: salted, pure and holy
p: Salt went with every offering, 'the salt of the covenant' (Leviticus 2:13).
b: Memullach, "salted," may mean the incense was mixed with salt, which makes it burn quickly and cleanly. Some scholars and older translations take it as "blended" or "mixed," from a related word for a sailor who mixes things. Every grain offering was salted with "the salt of your God's covenant" (Leviticus 2:13), and a lasting covenant is called "a covenant of salt" (Numbers 18:19; 2 Chronicles 13:5). Jesus tells his followers, "You are the salt of the earth" (Matthew 5:13), and "everyone will be salted with fire" (Mark 9:49).

a: I have called by name Bezalel
p: Bezalel means 'in God's shadow.' He is the grandson of Hur, who held up Moses' arms.
b: Betsal'el means "in the shadow (protection) of God." "Called by name" is the language God uses for prophets and leaders (Isaiah 43:1; 45:3), here used for an artist. His grandfather Hur held up Moses' arms with Aaron during the battle with Amalek (17:10–12) and helped judge the people while Moses was on the mountain (24:14). The Chronicler lists Bezalel in the family of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:18–20) and says Solomon worshiped at Bezalel's bronze altar (2 Chronicles 1:5). The Talmud says Bezalel "knew how to combine the letters by which heaven and earth were created" (Berakhot 55a).

a: I have filled him with the Spirit of God
t: The first person filled with God's Spirit
p: The Bible's first 'filled with the Spirit of God' is an artist. The phrase echoes creation.
b: Bezalel is the first person in the Bible said to be "filled with the Spirit of God," though the skilled weavers are already filled with "a spirit of wisdom" (28:3), and Pharaoh calls Joseph "a man who has the spirit of God in him" (Genesis 41:38). The phrase ruach Elohim last appeared over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2). The Talmud (Berakhot 55a) links Bezalel's three gifts, wisdom, understanding and knowledge, with the three by which God made the world in Proverbs 3:19–20, and Jon Levenson and others have built on this: the builder of the tabernacle is equipped as a small creator. Later the Spirit comes on judges, kings and prophets, and in Acts the believers "were filled, every one of them, with the Holy Spirit" (Acts 2:4).
orig: וָאֲמַלֵּא אֹתוֹ רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים (va'amalle oto ruach Elohim)
r: Genesis 1:2; 35:31; Proverbs 3:19–20; Judges 3:10; 1 Samuel 16:13; Isaiah 11:2; Acts 2:4

a: Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan
t: A great tribe and a small one
p: Rashi noted that Judah was the greatest tribe and Dan one of the lowest, yet both worked as equals.
b: Bezalel came from Judah, the royal tribe. Oholiab ("father's tent") came from Dan, which marched last in the camp (Numbers 10:25). Rashi, following the midrash, said this shows that God shows no favoritism: the great and the small built the sanctuary together (Rashi on 35:34). The pattern repeats at Solomon's temple, where the bronze worker Hiram was the son of a widow from Naphtali (1 Kings 7:13–14) or, in Chronicles, from Dan (2 Chronicles 2:13–14).

a: Make sure, though, that you keep my Sabbaths.
p: Akh, 'but' or 'above all,' taught the rabbis that building the tabernacle does not set aside the Sabbath.
b: The Sabbath command comes right after the building instructions and opens with akh, "but" or "only." Rashi explained: even though you are eager to build, the work must stop on the Sabbath. From this pairing (here and in 35:1–3) the rabbis derived the definition of "work" forbidden on the Sabbath: the 39 kinds of creative labor that were needed to build the tabernacle, such as sowing, weaving, writing, building and kindling (Mishnah, Shabbat 7:2; Talmud, Shabbat 49b). The building of God's dwelling defines what it means to rest.

a: this is a sign between me and you
p: The rainbow, circumcision and the Sabbath: three signs of three covenants.
b: The Torah names three signs (ot) of covenant: the rainbow for Noah (Genesis 9:12–13), circumcision for Abraham (Genesis 17:11), and the Sabbath for Israel. A sign is something visible that marks a relationship. Ezekiel repeats this verse almost word for word (Ezekiel 20:12, 20). The Sabbath set Israel apart in the ancient world. The Roman writer Seneca, as quoted by Augustine, mocked Jews for wasting a seventh of their lives in idleness. Paul writes that the Sabbath and festivals are "a shadow of things that were coming, but the body belongs to Christ" (Colossians 2:16–17), and most Christians came to keep the first day of the week instead.
r: Genesis 9:12–13; Genesis 17:11; Ezekiel 20:12; Ezekiel 20:20; Isaiah 56:4–6; Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10

a: Anyone who treats it as common must be put to death.
p: The penalty is harsh. Numbers 15 tells of one case. The rabbis made it almost impossible to carry out.
b: The verb chillel means to make common, to treat something holy as ordinary. Numbers 15:32–36 tells of a man stoned for gathering wood on the Sabbath. The rabbis kept the law in principle but surrounded it with conditions: two witnesses, a warning given just before the act, and the offender's stated acceptance of the penalty (Mishnah, Sanhedrin 5:1; 7:4). In practice capital punishment for Sabbath breaking was very rare. Christians have read the severity as a sign of how seriously God takes his covenant, while Jesus taught that "The Sabbath came into being for the sake of human beings, and not human beings for the sake of the Sabbath" (Mark 2:27).

a: a Sabbath, a day of total rest
p: Shabbat shabbaton, 'a sabbath of sabbath rest,' is Hebrew's way of saying 'total rest.'
b: Shabbat shabbaton doubles the word for emphasis, as "holy of holies" does (26:33). The phrase is used for the weekly Sabbath (16:23; 35:2) and for the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:31; 23:32), which Jewish tradition therefore calls "the Sabbath of Sabbaths." The verb shavat means to stop or cease. The Sabbath is first of all a stopping.

a: as a covenant for all time
p: Verses 16–17 are sung every Sabbath in the synagogue and at the Sabbath morning meal.
b: These two verses, beginning Veshamru ("They shall keep"), are among the best-known in Jewish worship. They are sung in the Friday evening service and recited before the Sabbath morning kiddush, the blessing over wine. The Mekhilta, the oldest rabbinic commentary on Exodus, reads "it is holy for you" (31:14) to mean that saving a life overrides the Sabbath: "The Sabbath is given to you, not you to the Sabbath," a saying close to Jesus' words in Mark 2:27. The Talmud also teaches that "if Israel kept two Sabbaths properly, they would be redeemed at once" (Talmud, Shabbat 118b).

a: he stopped and caught his breath
p: Vayinafash, from nefesh 'breath, soul,' is a bold picture. The rabbis drew from it the 'extra soul' of the Sabbath.
b: The verb vayinafash, related to nefesh, "breath, life, soul," means "to take a breath, be refreshed." It is used of a tired worker or a weary traveler (23:12; 2 Samuel 16:14). Applied to God it is startling, and translators often soften it ("rested"). Everett Fox's "paused for breath" is close to the Plain English. The point is not that God was tired (Isaiah 40:28) but that he made rest part of the world's rhythm. The Talmud (Beitzah 16a) reads it as a pun: God gives each person an "extra soul" on the Sabbath, and when the Sabbath ends, "woe (vay), the soul (nefesh) is gone."

a: stone tablets written by God's own finger
p: Pharaoh's magicians said 'This is the finger of God' (8:19). Jesus drove out demons 'by God's finger.'
b: "The finger of God" is a picture of God's direct action. Pharaoh's magicians used it when they could not copy the plague of gnats (8:19). Deuteronomy repeats that the tablets were "written by God's finger" (Deuteronomy 9:10). Jesus said, "If it is by God's finger that I throw out demons, then God's kingdom has already reached you" (Luke 11:20). Paul contrasts tablets of stone with a letter written "by the Spirit of the living God... on tablets that are hearts of flesh" (2 Corinthians 3:3), echoing Jeremiah 31:33. Jesus himself once wrote with his finger on the ground (John 8:6).

a: When he finished speaking with Moses on Mount Sinai
t: Which came first, the calf or the tabernacle?
p: Rashi said the tabernacle was commanded after the calf, as its cure. Ramban said the order is as written.
b: The tabernacle instructions (25–31) come before the golden calf (32), and the building (35–40) after it. Rashi, commenting on this verse, quotes the rabbinic rule that "there is no early and late in the Torah": the story of the calf happened many days before the command to build, and the tabernacle was given as a remedy, a way for God to dwell with a forgiven people. Ramban (on 35:1 and Leviticus 8:2) disagreed: the Torah follows the order of events unless it says otherwise, so God planned his dwelling before Israel sinned, and the calf nearly destroyed the plan. The first view makes the tabernacle a gift of forgiveness; the second makes it God's first intention, renewed after the sin. Many modern readers see the same contrast as a literary design: the right way to make a holy object, then the wrong way, then the right way again.

a: Moses was slow to come down from the mountain
p: The Talmud reads the Hebrew 'he delayed' as 'six had come': the people miscounted the forty days.
b: Moses had been gone forty days (24:18). The word boshesh, "he delayed," can be split into ba'u shesh, "six [hours] had come," and the Talmud (Shabbat 89a) builds on this. Moses had told the people he would return after forty days at the sixth hour, but they counted the day he went up, so they thought he was late. Then Satan showed them a picture of Moses lying dead in the sky, and they panicked. Rashi repeats this. The story tries to explain how a people who had just seen the sea split could fall so fast. The text itself says only that they waited and lost patience.

a: make us gods that will go ahead of us
p: Elohim can mean 'God' or 'gods.' The plural verb here says 'gods,' but Nehemiah retells it as 'your God.'
b: Elohim is the ordinary word for Israel's God and also for "gods." Here the verb "will go" is plural, so the people say "gods" (also 32:4, 8, 23, 31). Yet only one calf is made, and when Nehemiah 9:18 retells the story the words become singular: "This is your God who brought you up from Egypt." So the people may mean "a god" in a plural form, or the narrator may be mocking them by making their words plural. Ramban and Judah Halevi argued that the people did not want another god but a replacement for Moses, a visible guide "to go in front of us" (compare 13:21; 23:23).
orig: עֲשֵׂה־לָנוּ אֱלֹהִים אֲשֶׁר יֵלְכוּ (aseh-lanu elohim asher yelkhu)

a: Pull off the gold rings in the ears of your wives, your sons and your daughters
p: A midrash says the women would not give their earrings, so the men gave theirs, and the women were rewarded.
b: Aaron asks for the earrings of wives, sons and daughters, but in 32:3 "all the people" pull off "their" earrings. A midrash (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 45) says the women refused, and the men gave their own instead. As a reward, it says, the women received the New Moon (Rosh Chodesh) as a holiday of their own. Rashi suggests Aaron asked for the women's jewelry on purpose, hoping the delay would give Moses time to return. The gold rings probably came from Egypt (11:2; 12:35). Earrings were buried with household gods by Jacob's family long before (Genesis 35:4), and Gideon later made an idol from earrings taken as spoil (Judges 8:24–27).

a: shaped it with a tool
t: With a tool, or in a bag?
p: Cheret may be an engraving tool or a bag. Aaron either carved the gold or tied it up.
b: The phrase vayyatsar oto bacheret is usually read "he shaped it with an engraving tool," since cheret is a stylus in Isaiah 8:1. But the verb tsur can mean "tie up," and the same letters spell charit, "bag" (2 Kings 5:23). So Rashi gives both meanings, and some modern scholars read "he tied it up in a bag" (or "in a cloak") and then cast it. The second reading fits Aaron's later claim that he only threw the gold into the fire (32:24). The first fits "a calf of cast metal" (cast, then finished by hand). Either way the narrator says plainly that Aaron made it.

a: made it into a calf of cast metal
t: Bulls and gods in the ancient world
p: Canaanite El was called 'Bull,' Baal rode bulls, and Egypt worshiped the Apis bull. Which lies behind the calf?
b: An egel is a young bull, a symbol of strength and fertility. At Ugarit the high god El is called "Bull El," and the storm god Baal is linked with bulls. Small bronze bulls have been found in Israel, most famously the "Bull Site" figurine from the hills of Samaria (1100s BC). Egypt worshiped the Apis bull at Memphis, and Philo and some church fathers thought Israel copied Egypt. Most scholars today look to Canaanite images, because Israel's later calves at Bethel and Dan are clearly local (1 Kings 12:28–29). The honest verdict: the bull was a common sign of divine power across the region, and the calf drew on that shared language rather than on one particular god.

a: "These are your gods, Israel, that brought you up from the land of Egypt!"
p: Jeroboam said the same words over his calves at Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:28). Which story shaped which?
b: When the northern tribes broke away, King Jeroboam set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan and said, "Here are your gods, Israel, that brought you up from the land of Egypt!" (1 Kings 12:28), nearly the same words as here ("here" for "these"), also with a plural verb. Traditional readers see Jeroboam deliberately reviving Aaron's sin, and the narrator of Kings condemning him by the echo. Many critical scholars, such as Frank Moore Cross, think the influence ran the other way: the Exodus story was told (or retold) in Judah as an attack on the northern shrines, where priests may have claimed descent from Aaron. Both sides agree the two stories are meant to be read together. Psalm 106:20 sums up: "They traded their glory for the shape of an ox that feeds on grass."
r: 1 Kings 12:26–33; 2 Kings 10:29; Hosea 8:5–6; Hosea 10:5; Psalm 106:19–23; Nehemiah 9:18; Acts 7:40–41

a: "Tomorrow is a festival for the LORD!"
p: Aaron calls it a feast 'for the LORD.' The calf may have been meant as the LORD's image or his pedestal.
b: Aaron does not announce a feast for a new god but for YHWH, the LORD. So many interpreters think the people broke the second commandment rather than the first: they made an image to stand for the God who brought them out of Egypt (20:4–5, 23). William F. Albright suggested that the calf, like the cherubim, was meant as a pedestal on which the unseen God stood, since gods in Near Eastern art are often shown standing on bulls. If so, the difference from the ark was small in shape but huge in meaning: the ark was commanded, the calf was not; the cherubim were hidden, the calf was put on public display and worshiped (32:8).

a: they got up to play
p: Letsacheq can mean laughing, playing or sexual play. Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 10:7.
b: The verb tsachaq, the root of Isaac's name, means laugh or play. In Genesis it can carry a sexual sense (Isaac "fondling" Rebekah, Genesis 26:8; compare Genesis 39:14, 17). Rashi, following the midrash, says the word here hints at sexual immorality and even bloodshed. Others think it means singing, dancing and partying (32:18–19). Paul quotes the Greek of this verse: "The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play," and adds, "Do not become idol worshipers, as some of them did" (1 Corinthians 10:7). The Plain English keeps the vagueness of the Hebrew.

a: Your people, whom you brought up from the land of Egypt
p: God calls Israel 'your people' to Moses. Moses answers that they are 'your people' to God (32:11).
b: Until now God has called Israel "my people" (3:7; 5:1; 7:16). Here he says to Moses "your people, whom you brought up," as if disowning them. In his prayer Moses turns the words back: "why does your anger burn against your people? You brought them out from the land of Egypt" (32:11). The argument over a pronoun is the heart of the intercession. In 33:13 Moses presses again: "keep in mind that this nation is your people." By 34:9 God agrees to "take us as your own."

a: They have been quick to leave the path I commanded them.
p: Christian writers used the calf against the Jews. The rabbis read it as a lesson in repentance.
b: The Epistle of Barnabas (4:7–8; 14:1–4) argued that Israel lost the covenant at the calf, when Moses smashed the tablets, so it now belongs to Christians, and many church fathers repeated the charge. Jewish teachers answered in several ways. The Talmud (Avodah Zarah 4b–5a) says Israel was not the kind of people to do such a thing, and that it happened so that later generations would know a whole community can repent and be forgiven. Rashi, on "your people" in 32:7, says God meant the mixed crowd (erev rav) that left Egypt with Israel (12:38), whom Moses had accepted on his own. Modern Christian scholars have largely abandoned Barnabas's reading, noting that Exodus itself ends with the covenant renewed (34:10).

a: they are a stiff-necked people
p: A picture from farming: an ox that will not bend its neck to the yoke or turn when the farmer pulls.
b: Qesheh oref, "hard of neck," pictures a stubborn ox or donkey that stiffens its neck and will not let itself be steered. The phrase appears here for the first time in the Bible and becomes a refrain in this section (33:3, 5; 34:9) and in Deuteronomy (9:6, 13). Stephen uses it in his speech before his death: "Stiff-necked men, uncircumcised in your hearts and in your ears!" (Acts 7:51). The opposite picture is the yoke that is easy (Matthew 11:29–30).

a: So now leave me alone
p: Why would God ask Moses to leave him alone unless Moses could stop him? The rabbis heard an open door.
b: God has not been asked anything yet, but he says "leave me alone," as if Moses were already holding him back. The Talmud (Berakhot 32a) says this opened a door: God showed Moses that the matter depended on his prayer, and Moses seized God "like a man who grabs his friend by his garment." The offer "I will make you into a great nation" echoes the promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:2), and it is a real test: Moses could become a new Abraham. He refuses. Many Christian interpreters, such as Calvin, also see a test of Moses' love, and some modern theologians, such as Terence Fretheim, argue that God truly lets human prayer shape what he does.
r: Genesis 12:2; Genesis 18:22–33; Numbers 14:11–20; Deuteronomy 9:14; Psalm 106:23; Ezekiel 22:30

a: Moses begged the LORD his God to soften
p: Chillah penei means 'make the face soft or sweet,' an idiom for pleading with someone in power.
b: Vaychal et-penei YHWH uses an idiom for winning someone's favor, literally "to make the face weak, soft or pleasant." It is used of seeking a king's favor (Proverbs 19:6) and of praying to God (1 Samuel 13:12; Zechariah 7:2). The rabbis played on the similar verb chalah, "be sick": Moses prayed until he grew sick, or "released" God from his vow (Talmud, Berakhot 32a). Moses' three arguments follow: God's own act in the exodus (32:11), God's reputation among the nations (32:12), and God's oath to the fathers (32:13).

a: Why let the Egyptians say
p: Moses appeals to God's reputation. The argument returns in Numbers 14 and in Ezekiel.
b: The exodus was meant to show the Egyptians that "I am the LORD" (7:5; 14:4, 18). If God now destroys Israel, Moses argues, Egypt will say he rescued them only to kill them. Moses uses the same argument after the spies' report (Numbers 14:13–16) and again in Deuteronomy 9:28. Ezekiel turns it into a theme: God acts "for my name's sake, so that it would not be dishonored before the nations" (Ezekiel 20:9, 14; 36:22–23). Joshua asks, "What will you do for your great name?" (Joshua 7:9).

a: So the LORD changed his mind
p: Nicham can mean 'relent' or 'regret.' The Bible says both that God relents and that he does not.
b: The verb nicham (KJV "repented") means to change one's course, to relent or feel regret. Elsewhere Scripture says God "is not a human being who changes his mind" (Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29), and yet also that he relents when people turn (Jeremiah 18:7–10; Jonah 3:10; Joel 2:13). Classical Jewish and Christian theology (Maimonides, Aquinas, Calvin) holds that God's being and plan never change, and that such language is "accommodated" to human understanding. Many modern interpreters, such as Terence Fretheim, argue that the text means what it says: God has chosen to be moved by prayer. Both sides agree that Moses' prayer matters in the story.
r: Genesis 6:6; Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29; Jeremiah 18:7–10; Joel 2:13; Jonah 3:10; Jonah 4:2; Amos 7:3

a: the writing was God's writing, cut into the tablets
p: The Mishnah reads charut, 'engraved,' as cherut, 'freedom.' Only one who studies Torah is free.
b: Charut, "engraved," appears only here in the Bible. A famous saying in the Mishnah plays on it: "Do not read charut, engraved, but cherut, freedom, for no one is free except one who is busy with the study of Torah" (Mishnah, Avot 6:2). The Talmud also says the tablets were cut all the way through, so the closed letters mem and samekh had centers that floated in place by a miracle (Shabbat 104a). The verse stresses that the tablets were God's work from start to finish, which makes their destruction three verses later all the more shocking.

a: It is the sound of singing that I hear.
p: The verse plays on the verb 'anah, 'answer, sing,' and 'anah, 'be weak.' The last word is unclear.
b: Moses answers Joshua in a little poem built on one Hebrew root: "not the sound of 'anot of strength, not the sound of 'anot of weakness, the sound of 'annot I hear." The first two mean the shouts of victory and the cries of defeat, as in battle.
