The third is a different form of the verb and probably means singing, perhaps singing in turns, as in 15:21 where Miriam "answered" the women. The KJV says "them that sing." The Greek translators seem to have read something else here (see the variant).
orig: קוֹל עַנּוֹת אָנֹכִי שֹׁמֵעַ (qol 'annot anokhi shomea')

a: He threw the tablets down from his hands and smashed them
p: In the ancient world, breaking a treaty tablet cancelled the treaty. The rabbis said God praised Moses for it.
b: Moses may have acted in anger, as the text says his anger blazed. But the act also had a legal meaning. In Mesopotamian law "to break the tablet" meant to cancel a contract, and the people had broken the covenant they had sworn to keep (24:3, 7). Rashi, at the very end of the Torah, says that God approved: "Well done that you broke them" (Rashi on Deuteronomy 34:12; compare Talmud, Shabbat 87a). Jewish tradition holds that the broken pieces were kept in the ark beside the new tablets (Talmud, Bava Batra 14b). The day of the breaking is remembered as the fast of the 17th of Tammuz (Mishnah, Taanit 4:6).

a: He ground it until it was fine dust, scattered it on the water, and made the Israelites drink it
p: A Ugaritic myth has the goddess Anat destroy Death in the same steps. Deuteronomy omits the drinking.
b: Gold does not burn, so the steps are a total destruction told in traditional language. Samuel Loewenstamm showed that a Ugaritic poem from the 1300s BC describes the goddess Anat destroying the god Mot (Death) in almost the same sequence: she seizes him, splits him with a blade, burns him with fire, grinds him with millstones and scatters him in the field. Exodus may be using a known formula for wiping something out completely. Deuteronomy 9:21 repeats it but says Moses threw the dust into the stream that came down from the mountain, without the drinking. The Talmud (Avodah Zarah 44a) compares the drinking to the test of a wife suspected of unfaithfulness (Numbers 5:11–31): Israel, the bride, is tested.

a: I threw it in the fire, and out came this calf!
p: Aaron blames the people and the fire. The narrator has already said Aaron made it (32:4, 35).
b: Aaron's answer is almost comic: he blames the people ("they are set on evil") and then the fire, as if the calf made itself. The narrator has already told us that Aaron shaped it (32:4) and will say so again (32:35). Many readers, Jewish and Christian, see the story as a warning about leaders who give the crowd what it wants. The rabbis also defended Aaron: the Talmud (Sanhedrin 7a) says he saw Hur, who had been left in charge with him (24:14), killed for resisting the people, and feared that if they killed a priest too they could never be forgiven. Deuteronomy says God was angry enough with Aaron to destroy him, but Moses prayed for him (Deuteronomy 9:20).

a: the people were running wild
p: Para' means to let loose or let hair hang free. Proverbs 29:18 uses it: without vision the people run wild.
b: Parua' comes from a verb meaning to loosen, as when hair is let down (Leviticus 10:6) or a restraint thrown off. The people had cast off control, and Aaron had let it happen. The same verb is used in Proverbs 29:18: "Where there is no vision, the people run wild" (KJV, "the people perish"), a verse often misread as being about planning for the future. Its point is that without God's word, a people falls apart, as here.
orig: פָרֻעַ הוּא כִּי־פְרָעֹה אַהֲרֹן (farua' hu ki-fera'oh Aharon)

a: kill, each of you, his brother, his friend and his neighbor
p: This is one of the hardest scenes in the Bible. Readers have defended it, softened it and rejected it.
b: The Levites, Moses' own tribe, kill about three thousand people, and Moses says they have "filled their hands," that is, been ordained (32:29). Deuteronomy 33:9 praises Levi for putting God before father, mother and brothers, and Phinehas is praised for a similar act (Numbers 25:7–13). Traditional readers, Jewish and Christian, see a surgical judgment on the leaders of the revolt, without which the whole people would have perished (32:10). Some rabbis said only those who had worshiped the calf in front of witnesses were killed (Talmud, Yoma 66b). Many modern readers find the scene deeply troubling and read it as reflecting a later rivalry between priestly groups, or as a warning about religious violence rather than a model for it.

a: About three thousand of the people fell that day.
t: Three thousand at Sinai and Pentecost
p: About three thousand died after the calf. About three thousand were added to the church at Pentecost.
b: Jewish tradition came to link the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot) with the giving of the law at Sinai (see 19:1). Christian readers have noticed that on that same feast, Pentecost, the coming of the Spirit was followed by "about three thousand" people being baptized (Acts 2:41). The contrast fits Paul's words in 2 Corinthians 3:6–7: "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life," in a passage that goes on to discuss Moses' shining face (34:29–35). The New Testament does not draw this link itself; it is a reading many preachers have made.

a: It may be that I can make atonement for your sin.
p: Moses goes up to 'make atonement,' and then offers his own life. Paul echoes him in Romans 9:3.
b: Moses uses the priestly verb kipper, "make atonement," though he has no sacrifice. What he offers is himself: "But if not, wipe me out, please, from your book" (32:32). Paul says something like this about his own people: "I would even wish to be cursed myself, cut off from Christ, on behalf of my brothers, my relatives according to the flesh" (Romans 9:3). Christian readers have often seen Moses as a type of Christ, the mediator who stands between God and a sinful people (1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 3:1–6).

a: wipe me out, please, from your book that you have written
p: The first mention of God's book of the living. Moses' sentence breaks off before it is finished.
b: Moses' prayer breaks off: "if you will forgive their sin..." and he cannot finish. Then he asks to be erased from God's book. This is the first mention in the Bible of a heavenly record of the living, a list of citizens. It returns in Psalm 69:28 ("Let them be wiped out of the scroll of life"), Isaiah 4:3, Daniel 12:1, Malachi 3:16, Philippians 4:3 and Revelation 3:5; 20:12–15. Jewish tradition developed the picture of books opened on Rosh Hashanah and sealed on Yom Kippur (Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 16b). Moses risks his own name for theirs, and God refuses the trade (32:33).
r: 32:33; Psalm 69:28; Isaiah 4:3; Daniel 12:1; Malachi 3:16; Philippians 4:3; Revelation 3:5; Revelation 20:12–15

a: The one who has sinned against me is the one I will wipe out of my book.
t: No one can die for another's sin
p: God refuses Moses' offer. Each person answers for his own sin, as Ezekiel 18 later teaches.
b: God will not let Moses be erased in place of the guilty. The principle that each person bears his own sin appears in Deuteronomy 24:16 and becomes the theme of Ezekiel 18: "The one who sins, that one dies" (Ezekiel 18:4, 20). It stands in tension with 34:7, where the guilt of parents reaches their children, a tension the Bible itself works through (Jeremiah 31:29–30). Christian theology holds that what Moses could not do, Christ did: the sinless one died for others (2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 3:18).
r: 34:7; Deuteronomy 24:16; Jeremiah 31:29–30; Ezekiel 18:4; Ezekiel 18:20; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 3:18

a: I will hold them to account for their sin
t: A piece of the calf in every punishment
p: The rabbis said every later disaster carried a small share of the punishment for the calf.
b: The verb paqad means to visit, to look into, to settle accounts. God forgives enough to let the people go on, but the debt is not simply cancelled. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 102a) draws the lesson: "No punishment comes upon the world that does not have in it a small part of the punishment for the first calf." The calf became Israel's archetypal sin, as the fall of Adam became humanity's in Christian thought. The angel who will go ahead is the one promised in 23:20–23 (see there), not God's own presence; 33:2–3 and 33:14–15 take up the difference.

a: because they had made the calf. Aaron was the one who made it.
p: The verse says both that the people made it and that Aaron made it. Both are true in the story.
b: The Hebrew is awkward: "because they made the calf which Aaron made." Some translations smooth it out ("because of what they did with the calf Aaron had made"). The roughness is probably deliberate, or the sign of a story retold more than once. The people made it by demanding it and giving the gold; Aaron made it with his hands. Neither can hide behind the other. Many source critics think 32:35 is a separate tradition of the punishment, a plague, alongside the Levites' swords (32:28) and the bitter drink (32:20).
orig: עַל אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ אֶת־הָעֵגֶל אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה אַהֲרֹן (al asher asu et-ha'egel asher asah Aharon)

a: But I will not go up in your midst
p: God will keep his promise of the land but send an angel instead of going himself. Moses refuses the deal.
b: This is the low point of the story. God will still give the land, defeat the enemies and send an angel (33:2), but he will not go "among" them, the very thing the tabernacle was for (25:8; 29:45). The reason is mercy as much as anger: a holy God in the middle of a stubborn people would destroy them. The people grasp the meaning and mourn. Moses refuses to accept the land without God (33:15). Many readers see here the question at the heart of the Bible: is it enough to have God's gifts without God himself?

a: No one put on any of his jewelry.
p: The Talmud says angels had crowned every Israelite at Sinai, and after the calf the crowns were taken away.
b: The people strip off their ornaments in mourning and do not put them on again "from Mount Horeb on" (33:6). The Talmud (Shabbat 88a) imagines that when Israel said "we will do and we will listen" (24:7), 600,000 angels came down and tied two crowns on each Israelite, and after the calf these were removed. Some source critics have suggested that an older version of the story told what was done with the jewelry, perhaps making the ark or the tent, and that this was replaced by the priestly account of the people's gifts (35:22). The text as it stands lets the reader connect the removed ornaments with the gold brought for the tabernacle.

a: from Mount Horeb on
p: The same mountain has two names. Source critics link them to different sources; tradition sees two names for one place.
b: The mountain of God is called Horeb in some passages (3:1; 17:6; 33:6; most of Deuteronomy) and Sinai in others (19:1–23; 24:16; 31:18; 34:2). Source critics have assigned "Horeb" to the Elohist and Deuteronomic writers and "Sinai" to the Yahwist and Priestly ones. Traditional interpreters answer that one place can have two names, or that Horeb is the wider region. The name Horeb means "dry" or "waste." The mountain's location is debated; see the note on 19:1.

a: Moses used to take the tent and pitch it outside the camp
p: This tent stood outside the camp and had no priests. It seems to be different from the tabernacle.
b: The verbs here describe a habit: Moses "used to" pitch the tent, the cloud "would" come down. This tent stands outside the camp, has no priests or sacrifices, and is kept by Joshua (33:11), while the tabernacle stands in the middle of the camp (Numbers 2:2) and is kept by priests and Levites. Many critical scholars see an older tradition of a simple oracle tent, also found in Numbers 11:16–30; 12:4–10 and Deuteronomy 31:14–15. Traditional readers explain it as a temporary tent used before the tabernacle was built, moved outside because the camp had been defiled (so Rashi). Hebrews 13:13 calls Christians to "go out to him beyond the camp." See also 27:21.

a: The LORD spoke to Moses face to face
t: Face to face, yet not his face
p: 'Face to face' is an idiom for direct, personal speech. In 33:20 Moses still cannot see God's face.
b: "Face to face" (panim el-panim) describes direct conversation, with no dream, vision or go-between. Numbers 12:8 puts it "Mouth to mouth I speak with him, / openly and not in riddles," and Deuteronomy 34:10 says no prophet arose like Moses, "whom the LORD knew face to face." Nine verses later God says, "You cannot see my face" (33:20). Most interpreters, Jewish and Christian, take "face to face" as an idiom for closeness, not for seeing God's form. Some critics see two traditions side by side. Many Christian readers add that the one who spoke with Moses was the Son, "the one in the Father's embrace, who has made him known" (John 1:18).
r: 33:20; Genesis 32:30; Numbers 12:6–8; Deuteronomy 5:4; Deuteronomy 34:10; John 1:18; 1 Corinthians 13:12

a: his servant Joshua son of Nun, a young man, never left the inside of the tent
p: Joshua stays at the tent while Moses returns to camp: training for the day he will lead.
b: Joshua first appears as Moses' general against Amalek (17:9) and then as his assistant on the mountain (24:13; 32:17). Here the "young man" (na'ar, a word that can mean a servant of any age) stays at the tent when Moses leaves. The picture is of an apprentice who never leaves the place where God speaks. Numbers 27:18–23 and Deuteronomy 31:14–15 install him as Moses' successor at this same tent. The boy Samuel, lying near the ark at Shiloh when God calls him (1 Samuel 3:3), offers a similar scene.

a: 'I know you by name
p: To 'know' someone in Hebrew is to choose and care for them, not only to know facts.
b: The verb yada', "know," often means to choose, care for or be in relationship with someone (Genesis 18:19; Amos 3:2; Jeremiah 1:5). "I know you by name" means "I have singled you out." Moses repeats God's words back to him, then asks to "know" God in return (33:13). In the same way Jesus says, "I know my sheep, and my sheep know me," and the shepherd "calls his sheep by their names" (John 10:3, 14). Paul writes, "the Lord knows who belong to him" (2 Timothy 2:19).
r: 33:17; Genesis 18:19; Jeremiah 1:5; Amos 3:2; Isaiah 43:1; John 10:3; John 10:14; 2 Timothy 2:19

a: let me know your ways
p: Psalm 103:7: 'He let Moses know his ways.' Maimonides read the 'ways' as God's acts toward the world.
b: Moses asks first to know God's "ways" and only later to see his glory (33:18). Psalm 103:7–8 remembers the answer: "He let Moses know his ways; / he let the Israelites know his deeds. / Compassionate and gracious is the LORD, / slow to anger and great in loyal love," quoting 34:6. Maimonides argued that Moses was given knowledge of God's "attributes of action," the ways God acts toward the world (mercy, kindness, patience), not of God's essence, which no human can grasp, and that 34:6–7 lists those ways for people to imitate (Guide of the Perplexed 1.54).

a: "My face will go, and I will give you rest."
p: Panai, 'my face,' means God's own personal presence. Some read the line as a question.
b: "My face" (panai) means God himself, present in person, as opposed to an angel sent on his behalf (33:2). Most versions say "My Presence will go with you," but the Hebrew has no "with you"; the Plain English keeps "face" so that the reader can hear the link with "face to face" (33:11) and "You cannot see my face" (33:20). Isaiah 63:9 remembers that "the angel of his face saved them," and Deuteronomy 4:37 says God brought Israel out "with his face." A few interpreters read the line as a question ("Must my face go along?"), which would make Moses' reply in 33:15 a new appeal. "Rest" points to the promised land (Deuteronomy 12:9–10).

a: That is what will set us apart
p: Israel's distinctness is not its law or land but that God goes with it. The verb also marked the plagues.
b: The verb palah, "be distinct, set apart," was used in the plagues, when God made a distinction between Israel and Egypt (8:22; 9:4; 11:7). Moses argues that the only thing that makes Israel different from every other people is God going with them. Without that, they are just another tribe with a land. Christian writers have applied the verse to the church, whose mark is the presence of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16), and Jewish writers have read it as the basis of Israel's calling to be a people apart.

a: Please let me see your glory.
p: Readers have taken 'glory' as God's visible splendor, his very being, or his character.
b: Kavod, "glory," literally "weight," is the visible splendor of God's presence, seen as fire and cloud on Sinai (24:16–17) and later filling the tabernacle (40:34). Moses has already seen that. Many interpreters think he now asks for more: to see God as he is. Maimonides took it as a request to know God's essence. God answers with "goodness" and his name (33:19), so others read the request as a desire to know God's heart. John 1:14 answers from the Christian side: "We gazed at his glory, the kind of glory an only son has from his father, full of grace and truth," words that echo 34:6. At the transfiguration, Moses appears beside Jesus and sees his glory (Luke 9:30–32).

a: I will show grace to whoever I show grace, and pity whoever I pity
p: The pattern of 'I am who I am' (3:14). Paul quotes it in Romans 9:15 in the debate over election.
b: The words repeat their own verb, like God's name in 3:14, "I will be what I will be." They say that God's kindness is his own free choice and cannot be earned or demanded. Paul quotes the verse in Romans 9:15 to argue that God's mercy "is not a matter of the one who wills or the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy." Augustinian and Reformed readers find here the freedom of God in choosing whom to save; Arminian and many Catholic and Orthodox readers stress that the verse is about mercy toward the undeserving, not a decree against anyone. In Exodus its first effect is that a people who deserved destruction is forgiven.
orig: וְחַנֹּתִי אֶת־אֲשֶׁר אָחֹן וְרִחַמְתִּי אֶת־אֲשֶׁר אֲרַחֵם (vechannoti et-asher achon verichamti et-asher arachem)

a: no human being can see me and stay alive
t: No one can see God and live
p: Yet Jacob, Gideon's parents and Isaiah say they saw God and lived. The Bible holds both.
b: The belief that seeing God means death runs through the Bible, and so does the surprise of those who survive it: Jacob at Peniel (Genesis 32:30), Manoah and his wife (Judges 13:22), Isaiah in the temple (Isaiah 6:5). The elders of Israel "saw the God of Israel" on the mountain and were not harmed (24:10–11; see there). The New Testament affirms both sides: "Nobody has ever seen God" (John 1:18; 1 Timothy 6:16), yet "those whose hearts are pure... will see God" (Matthew 5:8) and "they will see his face" in the new creation (Revelation 22:4; 1 John 3:2).
r: Genesis 16:13; Genesis 32:30; 24:10–11; Judges 6:22–23; Judges 13:22; Isaiah 6:5; John 1:18; 1 Timothy 6:16; Matthew 5:8; 1 John 3:2; Revelation 22:4

a: I will set you in a crack in the rock
p: Elijah later stood in 'the cave' on the same mountain. The hymn 'Rock of Ages' draws on this verse.
b: Centuries later Elijah fled to Horeb, spent the night in "the cave," and stood at its mouth while the LORD "passed by," not in the wind, earthquake or fire, but in a quiet sound (1 Kings 19:8–13). The rabbis thought it was the same crack where Moses stood, one of the things created on the evening of the first Sabbath (Talmud, Pesachim 54a; Mishnah, Avot 5:6 has a similar list). Augustus Toplady's hymn "Rock of Ages, cleft for me" (1776) reads the rock as Christ, struck to shelter sinners, an idea drawn from Paul's "the rock was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4).

a: You will see my back
p: The Talmud, Maimonides, Gregory of Nyssa and Luther each read God's 'back' differently.
b: Readers have always known this is a picture, since God has no body (Deuteronomy 4:15). The Talmud (Berakhot 7a) says Moses saw the knot of God's tefillin at the back of his head, a bold way of saying he saw God's bond with Israel. Maimonides read achor, "back," as "what follows from" God: his works and effects, not his essence (Guide 1.38). Gregory of Nyssa said that to see God's back is to follow him, since one who follows sees the back of the leader (Life of Moses, book 2). Luther, in his Heidelberg Disputation (1518), spoke of the "back parts of God," God known through suffering and the cross rather than by direct sight.

a: Cut out two tablets of stone for yourself, like the first ones
p: God made the first tablets; Moses must cut the second. The rabbis said the chips made him rich.
b: The first tablets were "God's work" (32:16). The second are cut by Moses, though God still writes on them (34:1; Deuteronomy 10:1–4). Many readers see a lesson here: a renewed covenant asks more of the human partner. Deuteronomy 10:1–3 adds that Moses first made a wooden ark to hold them. The Talmud, playing on pesal lekha, "cut for yourself," says the leftover chips were Moses' to keep, and that the stone was sapphire, so Moses became rich (Nedarim 38a). The rabbis also taught that the broken first tablets were kept in the ark beside the new ones (see 32:19).

a: he called out the name of the LORD
p: The Hebrew does not say whether God or Moses called out the name. Readers differ.
b: The verse says "he stood with him there, and he called on (or: called out) the name of the LORD." The subject could be Moses, who "called on the name of the LORD" in worship, as Abraham did (Genesis 12:8), and the KJV leaves it open. Or it could be God, keeping his promise in 33:19: "I will call out the name of the LORD before you." Most modern interpreters take God as the speaker, since in the next verse the LORD passes by and "calls out" the same name. The Plain English follows that reading but keeps the Hebrew "he."

a: "The LORD, the LORD, a God compassionate and gracious
p: Jewish tradition counts thirteen 'attributes of mercy' in 34:6–7 and recites them on fast days and festivals.
b: The rabbis counted thirteen middot, "attributes," in these verses, and they are the center of Jewish prayers for forgiveness. The Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 17b) says God wrapped himself in a prayer shawl like a prayer leader and showed Moses this order of prayer: "Whenever Israel sins, let them say this before me and I will forgive them." They are chanted in the Selichot prayers before the High Holy Days, many times on Yom Kippur, and on festivals when the Torah is taken out. The rabbis' count stops at venaqqeh, "and acquits" (see the note on 34:7), turning the verse into a pure statement of mercy.

a: compassionate and gracious
t: A mother's love and a free gift
p: Rachum comes from rechem, 'womb.' Channun means showing favor no one has earned.
b: Rachum, "compassionate," comes from rechem, "womb": the tender love of a mother for the child she bore (Isaiah 49:15). Channun, "gracious" or "kind," is the giving of favor that is not owed (33:19, "I will show grace to whoever I show grace"). Both words are used almost only of God in the Bible. They answer the calf directly: the people deserve destruction, and God names himself first by mercy.

a: slow to anger
p: In Hebrew anger is 'nostrils' or 'heat.' A patient God is 'long of nostrils,' slow to heat up.
b: Hebrew pictures anger as hot, flaring nostrils (af), as in "my anger can burn" (32:10). The phrase erekh appayim, "long of nostrils," describes someone who takes a long time to get hot, a patient person. Proverbs praises the same quality in people: "Being slow to anger is better than being a mighty soldier" (Proverbs 16:32). The rabbis noted that the plural "nostrils" can mean God is patient with both the righteous and the wicked (Talmud, Eruvin 22a).

a: great in loyal love and faithfulness
p: Hesed and emet, 'loyal love and faithfulness,' stand behind John's 'full of grace and truth' (John 1:14).
b: Chesed is love that keeps faith with a relationship, the word Ruth uses for Boaz's kindness (Ruth 2:20; 3:10). Emet is faithfulness, reliability, truth. Together they describe a God who keeps his promises. John's prologue seems to echo this scene: Moses could not see God's face, but "the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us. We gazed at his glory... full of grace and truth," and "grace and truth arrived through Jesus Christ" (John 1:14, 17–18). Many scholars think John's "grace and truth" translates this Hebrew pair.
r: Genesis 24:27; Ruth 3:10; Psalm 25:10; Psalm 86:15; John 1:14; John 1:17–18

a: The LORD passed in front of him and called out
t: The Bible's favorite description of God
p: These verses are quoted or echoed more than any other description of God in the Hebrew Bible.
b: No passage about God's character is repeated more often in the Hebrew Bible. Moses quotes it back to God after the spies (Numbers 14:18). The Psalms sing it (Psalm 86:15; 103:8; 145:8). Joel calls the people to return because of it (Joel 2:13). Nehemiah's great prayer rests on it (Nehemiah 9:17). Jonah complains that he fled because he knew God was like this (Jonah 4:2), and Nahum turns its second half against Nineveh (Nahum 1:3). Many scholars call it Israel's earliest creed about who God is.
r: Numbers 14:18; Nehemiah 9:17; Psalm 86:15; Psalm 103:8; Psalm 145:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Nahum 1:3; 2 Chronicles 30:9

a: keeping loyal love to thousands
p: Love reaches 'thousands' (generations), punishment three or four. Mercy outweighs judgment.
b: "Thousands" most likely means thousands of generations, as Deuteronomy 7:9 says outright: "He keeps his covenant and his loyal love for a thousand generations." Set beside punishment reaching "the third and the fourth generation," the contrast is deliberate: God's love outlasts his judgment by far. Rashi, on the matching verse 20:6, computed that God's goodness is five hundred times greater than his punishment. The same pair appears in the Ten Commandments (20:5–6).

a: Yet he will by no means leave guilt unpunished.
p: The Hebrew doubles the verb for emphasis. The rabbis split the phrase and read 'he clears' those who repent.
b: The Hebrew venaqqeh lo yenaqqeh is literally "and acquitting, he will not acquit," a doubled verb that means "he will by no means leave unpunished." The KJV adds the words "the guilty," which are not in the Hebrew. Targum Onkelos already splits the phrase: God forgives "those who return to his Torah" and does not clear "those who do not return." The Talmud (Yoma 86a) reads it the same way: God clears those who repent and not those who do not. That is why the Jewish liturgy quotes the verse only to venaqqeh, "and acquits," ending the thirteen attributes on forgiveness. The plain sense holds mercy and justice together: God forgives, yet sin is not ignored.

a: to the third and the fourth generation
p: Does God punish innocent children? The Targum and Talmud say only when children repeat their parents' sins.
b: The phrase troubled ancient readers as much as modern ones, since Deuteronomy 24:16 and Ezekiel 18 insist that each person answers for his own sin. Targum Onkelos and the Talmud (Berakhot 7a; Sanhedrin 27b) explain that children suffer only when they hold on to their parents' deeds. Many modern scholars note that three or four generations often lived in one household, so the verse describes how a family head's sin damages everyone living under his roof, rather than a curse on future descendants. Others see a real development within the Bible, from family responsibility to individual responsibility (Jeremiah 31:29–30). The matching verse in the Ten Commandments adds "of those who hate me" (20:5).
r: 20:5; Numbers 14:18; Deuteronomy 24:16; Jeremiah 31:29–30; Ezekiel 18:2–4; Ezekiel 18:20; John 9:2–3

a: Yes, this is a stiff-necked people
p: The word ki can mean 'though' or 'because.' Moses may be turning God's reason into an argument.
b: God said he would not go among the people because (ki) they were stiff-necked (33:3, 5). Moses now uses the same words: "go among us, ki this is a stiff-necked people." Most versions read "although." But ki usually means "for, because," and several interpreters, including Walter Moberly, think Moses is arguing boldly: precisely because they are stubborn, they need you among them, or they will never change. The forgiveness of 34:6–7 makes this possible.

a: Here I am, making a covenant.
p: Is this a new covenant or the old one restored? Its terms repeat parts of chapters 20–23.
b: The broken covenant is restored on new terms. Its laws (34:11–26) repeat parts of the earlier "book of the covenant" almost word for word, especially the festivals (23:14–19). Traditional readers see a renewal of the same covenant, now resting on God's forgiveness. Critical scholars often see an older, separate covenant text (from the source called J) placed here by the editors. The promise of "wonders that have never been created" uses bara, the verb of Genesis 1:1, used in the Bible only for God's acts. Jeremiah later promises a "new covenant" written on hearts, "It will not be like the covenant I cut with their ancestors... They broke that covenant of mine" (Jeremiah 31:31–34).

a: cut down their Asherah poles
p: Asherah was a Canaanite mother goddess and a wooden symbol of her. Some Israelites linked her with the LORD.
b: In Ugaritic texts Athirat (Asherah) is the wife of the high god El. In the Bible asherah usually means a wooden pole or tree set up beside an altar as her symbol, so it can be "cut down." Inscriptions from Kuntillet Ajrud in Sinai (about 800 BC) bless people "by YHWH of Samaria and by his asherah," and a tomb inscription from Khirbet el-Qom says something similar. Scholars debate whether "his asherah" means the goddess as the LORD's consort or a cult object, but the finds show why the prophets fought so hard against her (1 Kings 15:13; 2 Kings 21:7; 23:4–7).
r: Deuteronomy 7:5; Deuteronomy 16:21; Judges 6:25–30; 1 Kings 15:13; 1 Kings 18:19; 2 Kings 21:7; 2 Kings 23:4–7

a: the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God
p: Qanna is the jealousy of a husband who will not share his wife. It is love that demands loyalty.
b: Qanna, "jealous," is used in the Bible only of God. It is the burning devotion of a husband who will not share his marriage with a rival, which is why the next verses speak of Israel "chasing after" other gods like an unfaithful wife (34:15–16). In English "jealous" can sound petty, so some translate "zealous" or "passionate." Here it is even God's name. Paul uses the same picture of the church: "I am jealous for you with a jealousy that is God's own. I arranged for you to be engaged to one husband, so that I could present you to Christ as a pure virgin" (2 Corinthians 11:2).
r: 20:5; Deuteronomy 4:24; Deuteronomy 5:9; Joshua 24:19; Nahum 1:2; 2 Corinthians 11:2; James 4:5

a: When they go chasing after their gods like prostitutes
p: Zanah, 'act as a prostitute,' becomes the prophets' picture of idolatry as adultery against God.
b: The verb zanah means to act as a prostitute or to be sexually unfaithful. Here, for the first time in the Bible, it describes worshiping other gods. The image grows into one of the prophets' great themes: Israel is the LORD's bride, and idolatry is adultery (Hosea 1–3; Jeremiah 3:1–10; Ezekiel 16; 23). It may also reflect real sexual rites connected with some Canaanite worship, though how common such rites were is debated. The warning about marrying into the land's peoples (34:16) returns in Deuteronomy 7:3–4 and in Solomon's story (1 Kings 11:1–8).
r: 34:16; Leviticus 17:7; Deuteronomy 7:3–4; Hosea 1:2; Jeremiah 3:1–10; Ezekiel 16:15–34; 1 Kings 11:1–8

a: Keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread.
p: Verses 18–26 repeat the festival laws of 23:12–19, nearly word for word.
b: The laws in 34:18–26 repeat, with small changes, the festival calendar of 23:14–19 (see the notes there), the firstborn laws of 13:12–13 and the Sabbath of 23:12. Repeating the terms is what a renewed treaty does. A new emphasis is the Sabbath even "at plowing time and at harvest" (34:21), the busiest seasons of a farmer's year. The three pilgrimage feasts are Unleavened Bread (Passover week), Weeks (Shavuot, Pentecost) and Gathering (Sukkot, Booths).

a: No one is to appear before my face with empty hands.
t: To see God's face, or to be seen?
p: The vowels say 'my face will not be seen,' but the consonants may first have read 'they shall not see my face.'
b: In this verse and in 23:15; 34:23–24 the Masoretic vowels read the verb as passive: "appear before me" or "be seen." Many scholars, beginning with Abraham Geiger in the 1800s, think the consonants were first read as active: "see my face." Pilgrims would go to "see the face of the LORD" at his shrine (compare Psalm 42:2). Scribes, troubled by 33:20 ("no human being can see me and stay alive"), may have changed the vowels out of reverence. Either way, the Hebrew idiom means coming to worship at the sanctuary. The Plain English, like 23:15, says "appear before my face" to keep the image.

a: Do not boil a young goat in the milk of its mother.
p: This rule appears three times in the Torah. The rabbis built the laws of meat and milk on it.
b: This is the second of three times the rule appears (23:19; Deuteronomy 14:21). See the note on 23:19 for its possible meanings. The Talmud reasons that a law repeated three times must forbid three things: cooking meat with milk, eating them together, and profiting from such a mixture (Chullin 115b). From this grew the Jewish practice of keeping meat and dairy foods, dishes and meals separate, one of the most visible parts of keeping kosher.
l: Milk and meat in Jewish law
Milk and meat in Jewish law

a: Bread he did not eat, and water he did not drink.
p: Moses fasts forty days twice (Deuteronomy 9:9, 18). Elijah and Jesus also fast forty days.
b: Deuteronomy says Moses fasted forty days and nights both times he was on the mountain (Deuteronomy 9:9, 18). Elijah travels forty days and nights to the same mountain on the strength of one meal (1 Kings 19:8). Jesus fasts forty days in the wilderness before his ministry, and answers the tempter with words from Deuteronomy (Matthew 4:1–11). At the transfiguration Moses and Elijah, the two who fasted forty days and met God at Horeb, appear with him (Matthew 17:3). Going without water for forty days is beyond human strength, which is the narrator's point.

a: And he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the Ten Words.
t: Which ten, and who wrote them?
p: 34:1 says God will write. 34:27–28 seem to say Moses wrote. And are the 'Ten Words' those of chapter 20?
b: This is the first time the Bible uses the phrase aseret ha-devarim, "the ten words," from which comes "Decalogue." Two questions follow. First, who wrote? God promised to write (34:1; Deuteronomy 10:2–4), but the nearest subject is Moses (34:27). Most traditional readers say "he" is God, as in 34:1. Second, which ten? Deuteronomy says the second tablets held the same words as the first (Deuteronomy 10:4). But in 1773 Goethe argued that the ten words here are the laws just given in 34:14–26, a "ritual decalogue," and Wellhausen and many critics followed him. Jewish and Christian tradition holds that the tablets bore the Ten Commandments of 20:2–17.

a: the skin of his face was shining
p: Qaran, 'shone,' is related to qeren, 'horn.' Jerome's Latin said Moses' face was 'horned.'
b: The verb qaran appears only here (34:29, 30, 35). It is related to qeren, "horn," and may picture rays spreading like horns (Habakkuk 3:4). The Greek and the Targums read "shone" or "was glorified." Aquila and Jerome's Vulgate wrote "horned" (cornuta), which Jerome took as a sign of glory, and Michelangelo's Moses (about 1515) has horns. Some scholars recall the horned crowns of gods in Near Eastern art. William Propp argued that the skin itself became hard, like horn, a disfigurement rather than a glow. Ruth Mellinkoff showed that the horns began as a mark of honor; only later did they merge with the slander, traced by Joshua Trachtenberg, that Jews had horns.

a: Moses came down from Mount Sinai
p: Rabbinic chronology puts this descent on the tenth of the seventh month: the first Day of Atonement.
b: Jewish tradition worked out the calendar from the forty-day periods. Moses went up on the seventh of Sivan, broke the tablets on the seventeenth of Tammuz, interceded forty days, went up again on the first of Elul, and came down with the second tablets and God's forgiveness on the tenth of Tishri (Seder Olam; Rashi on 33:11). That day became Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, a day of forgiveness for all time. This is why the month of Elul is a season of repentance, and why the Thirteen Attributes (34:6–7) are central to Yom Kippur prayer. The Bible itself does not give these dates.

a: he put a veil over his face
p: Paul says Moses veiled his face so Israel would not see the glory fade. Exodus does not say it faded.
b: In Exodus, Moses wears the veil among the people and removes it before God, apparently so that the people can bear to be near him (34:30–31). Hugo Gressmann and Thomas Dozeman compare the masks of priests in other religions: the veil marks Moses' face as an office, the face through which God speaks. Paul reads the scene in 2 Corinthians 3:7–18: Moses veiled himself "so that the Israelites would not look steadily at the end of what was being set aside" (2 Corinthians 3:13). Older versions render the verb "fading," but Scott Hafemann argues that katargeō means "set aside, made ineffective," not "fade." Paul adds that a veil still covers hearts when Moses is read, and is taken away when one turns to the Lord. Jewish readers answer that Moses' glory never faded (Deuteronomy 34:7).

a: Moses gathered the whole community
p: The same verb, qahal, was used when the people gathered around Aaron to demand the calf (32:1).
b: The synagogue reading for 35:1–38:20 is named Vayaqhel, "he gathered," after this verb. In 32:1 the people "gathered" (vayyiqqahel) around Aaron to make the calf. Now Moses gathers them to make the sanctuary. The same crowd, the same gold, the same eagerness, turned toward the right end. Rashi dates this assembly to the day after Moses came down on Yom Kippur (see the note on 34:29). From qahal, "assembly," comes qehillah, a Jewish congregation, and in the Greek Bible the matching word is ekklēsia, which the New Testament uses for "church."

a: you must not kindle a fire in any of your homes
p: Karaites and Samaritans kept no fire burning at all. The rabbis forbade lighting, not having, a fire.
b: This is the only specific Sabbath work named in the Torah besides gathering food and wood (16:23–29; Numbers 15:32). The Karaites, a Jewish movement that rejected rabbinic tradition, read it strictly and sat in darkness and cold through the Sabbath, as Samaritans long did too. The rabbis read it as forbidding the act of kindling, not the presence of fire, so lamps lit before sunset may keep burning. The Friday evening candles of Jewish homes, lit just before the Sabbath begins, became a sign of that reading. The Talmud also asks why fire alone is singled out and gives several answers (Shabbat 70a).

a: Men came along with the women
p: The text stresses that women gave jewelry and did skilled work. Their part in building the sanctuary is named twice.
b: The narrator goes out of the way to include women: "Men came along with the women" (35:22), every "skilled woman" spinning yarn (35:25–26), and "every man and woman" giving (35:29). Women also give the bronze mirrors for the basin (38:8). Carol Meyers has argued that textile work was an area of women's skill and authority in ancient Israel, so these verses record a real public role for women in the building of the shrine. The jewelry listed includes chach, probably a brooch or pin, and kumaz, perhaps a necklace of gold beads.

a: spun the goat hair
p: The Talmud says the women spun the goat hair while it was still on the goats.
b: The words "whose hearts lifted them with skill" suggested to the rabbis a special skill beyond ordinary spinning. The Talmud (Shabbat 74b, 99a) and Rashi say the women spun the goat hair directly from the backs of the living goats, a feat of great skill. Whatever one thinks of the story, it reflects admiration for the women's craftsmanship. The black goat-hair cloth formed the tent over the tabernacle (26:7).

a: he has given him the gift of teaching
p: This is the one detail chapter 31 did not mention: Bezalel and Oholiab could teach their skills.
b: Chapter 35 repeats Bezalel's call almost exactly (compare 31:2–6), but adds that God "put it in his heart to teach" (ulehorot natan belibbo). The verb horah, "teach," is the root of Torah, "teaching." Great skill is not enough: the work needs people who can pass it on. Jewish and Christian writers alike have used this verse to honor teachers of craft as well as teachers of Scripture.

a: just as the LORD has commanded
p: The Hebrew can be read as the end of Moses' speech ('they are to do') or as narrative ('so they did').
b: The verb ve'asah can be read as a future ("Bezalel and Oholiab will work") ending Moses' words in 35:30–35, or as a past ("So Bezalel and Oholiab worked") beginning the story of the work. The KJV and the Plain English take it as part of the speech, which closes with "as the LORD has commanded." Many modern versions start the narrative here. The meaning is the same either way: the work begins with the skilled people God has gifted.

a: The people are bringing too much
p: The only time in the Bible people are told to stop giving. Their eagerness for the calf is now turned to good.
b: The craftsmen leave their work to report that there is too much, and Moses sends word through the camp to stop (36:6). It is the only appeal in the Bible to stop giving. The same people who gave their gold at once for the calf (32:2–3) now give their gold for the sanctuary, without being asked twice. Paul praises the Macedonians who gave "what they could, and beyond what they could. They chose it on their own" (2 Corinthians 8:3), and David's people later gave so freely for the temple that they "rejoiced" (1 Chronicles 29:9).

a: All the skilled at heart among those doing the work made the tabernacle
p: Chapters 36–39 repeat chapters 26–28 almost word for word. Ancient building accounts did the same.
b: Modern readers often skip these chapters, which repeat the earlier instructions in the past tense. But ancient temple-building accounts follow the same pattern: a divine command, the gathering of materials, the building, the dedication, and the god taking up residence. Victor Hurowitz compared Gudea of Lagash's account of building Ningirsu's temple (about 2100 BC), Ugaritic stories of Baal's palace, Assyrian royal inscriptions and Solomon's temple (1 Kings 5–8). The repetition shows obedience: every detail God asked for was done. The Talmud adds that the building order here (tent first, then the ark) differs from the command order (ark first), and has Bezalel point out that one builds a house before furnishing it (Berakhot 55a).

a: For the tabernacle he made frames of acacia wood that stood upright.
t: The frames the Greek leaves out
p: The Greek building account has no frames, bars or goat-hair tent. See the variant on 36:8.
b: Verses 36:14–34, the goat-hair tent, its coverings, the frames, their bases and the bars, have no counterpart in the Greek account of the building, although the Greek of chapter 26 describes them all. The Hebrew order here also differs from the commands: the tent comes before the ark, which Bezalel makes only in 37:1. On why the Greek is shorter and ordered differently, see the variant on 36:8; on the change of order in the Hebrew, see the note on 37:1.

a: Bezalel made the ark of acacia wood
p: Bezalel's name stands at the head of the furnishings. The midrash says the ark bears his name for his devotion.
b: In the building account most verbs say "he made" without a name, or "they made." Bezalel's name stands at the head of the furnishings, starting with the ark. Rashi, following the midrash, says the ark is linked with Bezalel's name because he gave himself to it more than anyone else did. Deuteronomy 10:3 says Moses made a wooden ark for the second tablets. Traditional readers have harmonized the two (a temporary chest, or Moses as the one who had it made); critical scholars see two separate traditions.

a: He made the altar of incense of acacia wood.
p: The Septuagint's building account does not mention making the incense altar at all.
b: In the Hebrew the incense altar is made after the lampstand (37:25–28), as it was commanded in 30:1–5. The Septuagint's account of the building never mentions making it, though the Greek mentions the altar elsewhere (Greek 40:5, 26). This is one of the clearest signs that the Greek of chapters 35–40 rests on, or produced, a differently shaped text. See the variant on 36:8 for the wider picture, and the note on 26:35 for the altar's odd place in the instructions.

a: from the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance of the tent of meeting
p: Rashi tells that Moses did not want the women's mirrors, but God said they were dearest of all.
b: Ancient mirrors were polished bronze, and Egyptian women were famous for them. Who were "the women who served"? The verb tsava' is used of Levites' service (Numbers 4:23) and of troops; The Hebrew (Masoretic) text of 1 Samuel 2:22 also mentions women "who served at the entrance of the tent of meeting" at Shiloh, though the Plain there follows the shorter text without that clause (see the variant note on 1 Samuel 2:22). The Septuagint calls them women "who fasted," and Targum Onkelos women "who came to pray." Rashi, following the midrash Tanhuma, says Moses at first rejected the mirrors as tools of vanity, but God told him: "Accept them, for these are dearer to me than everything," because in Egypt the women had used them to win back their exhausted husbands and keep Israel's families alive.

a: Here is the account of the tabernacle
p: Pequdei, 'the counts,' gives the last Torah portion of Exodus its name. The leaders publish their accounts.
b: Pequdei, from paqad, "count, record," names the last reading of Exodus (38:21–40:38). The materials are counted publicly under the Levite Ithamar. The midrash (Exodus Rabbah 51) says Moses gave a full account so that no one could suspect him of keeping any gold, and draws the lesson that those who handle public funds must be above suspicion. Compare Paul's care to handle the collection for Jerusalem, in his words, "We are guarding against this: that anyone could blame us over the large gift we are handling" (2 Corinthians 8:20–21).

a: twenty-nine talents and 730 shekels
p: About a ton of gold, three and a half tons of silver and two and a half tons of bronze.
b: A talent was 3,000 shekels (see the next note), roughly 75 pounds or 34 kilograms. So the gold weighed about a ton, the silver about 3½ tons, and the bronze about 2½ tons. Critical scholars see these figures as part of the priestly writers' idealized picture. Defenders note that the Israelites left Egypt with Egyptian silver and gold (12:35–36), and Kenneth Kitchen compared the gifts of Egyptian kings to their temples, which were far larger: Osorkon I (about 920 BC) claimed to have given hundreds of tons of gold and silver. Either way, the figures add up exactly, which the next verse shows.

p: 603,550 half shekels equal 100 talents and 1,775 shekels exactly, if a talent is 3,000 shekels.
b: Half a shekel from 603,550 men is 301,775 shekels. The text says the silver was 100 talents and 1,775 shekels (38:25). The two agree exactly if a talent is 3,000 shekels, which is the standard known from other ancient sources. The figure 603,550 is the same as the census of Numbers 1:46, taken a month after the tabernacle was set up (40:17; Numbers 1:1). Whether such a number of men, implying two million people or more, could have lived in Sinai is a long-running debate. See the note on 12:37 for the main proposals, including reading elef ("thousand") as a military unit or clan.

a: just as the LORD had commanded Moses
p: The refrain 'just as the LORD had commanded Moses' comes exactly seven times in chapter 39 and seven in chapter 40.
b: The phrase ka'asher tsivah YHWH et-Mosheh marks the end of each stage of the work: seven times in the making of the priests' clothes (39:1, 5, 7, 21, 26, 29, 31) and seven times in the setting up of the tabernacle (40:19, 21, 23, 25, 27, 29, 32). The double seven echoes the seven days of creation and the seven speeches that gave the instructions (see the note on 25:1). The message is simple: where the calf was Israel's own idea, the sanctuary is built exactly as God said.
orig: כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה אֶת־מֹשֶׁה (ka'asher tsivah YHWH et-Mosheh)

a: They beat the gold into thin sheets, and he cut them into threads
p: The oldest known description of making gold thread: beaten foil cut into strips and woven in.
b: This verse describes a technique known from the ancient world: gold was beaten into foil, cut into narrow strips and then woven or embroidered into cloth with colored yarn. Gold-wrapped threads and gold strips have been found in textiles from Egypt and Mesopotamia. In the instructions this detail was not mentioned (28:6). The ephod would have shimmered as the priest moved. Psalm 45:13 pictures a royal bride whose "clothing is woven with gold."

a: So all the work for the tabernacle of the tent of meeting was finished.
t: Finished, like the heavens and the earth
p: 'Was finished' echoes Genesis 2:1: 'the heavens and the earth were finished.'
b: The verb vattekhel, "was finished," matches Genesis 2:1, "the heavens and the earth were finished (vaykhullu)." It is one of several deliberate echoes of the creation story at the end of Exodus. The others follow: Moses "saw" all the work (39:43; Genesis 1:31), Moses "blessed" (39:43; Genesis 2:3), and Moses "finished the work" (40:33; Genesis 2:2). Solomon's temple is finished with similar words (1 Kings 7:51). See the note on 39:43.

a: Moses saw all the work, and there it was: they had done it.
p: Moses 'saw' the work, 'and look,' and 'blessed' them, as God saw and blessed in Genesis 1–2.
b: Genesis 1:31 says, "God looked at everything he had made, and there it was, very good." Here Moses sees all the work, "and there it was: they had done it." God blessed the seventh day (Genesis 2:3); Moses blesses the people. Joseph Blenkinsopp, Jon Levenson, Moshe Weinfeld and many others have argued that the priestly writers deliberately shaped the tabernacle story as a new creation: the world was God's first temple, and the tabernacle is a world in small, where order is restored after the chaos of the calf. Some Christian readers carry the line forward to the new creation, where "God's tent is with human beings" (Revelation 21:3–5). Readers who doubt the pattern grant the verbal echoes but think they are not as systematic as claimed.

a: And Moses blessed them.
p: Rashi says Moses prayed that the Shekhinah would rest on their work. The words became Psalm 90:17.
b: The text does not say what Moses said. Rashi, following the midrash, gives the words: "May it be his will that the Shekhinah rest on the work of your hands," and adds that Moses also said, "Let the kindness of the Lord our God be on us. Give the work of our hands firm footing for us" (Psalm 90:17). The psalm is the only one headed "A prayer of Moses, the man of God" (Psalm 90:0). The next chapter shows the blessing answered: the glory fills the tabernacle (40:34).

a: On the first day of the first month
p: The tabernacle goes up on New Year's Day, one year after the exodus. Noah's ark was opened on the same date.
b: The first month is the month of the exodus (12:2). So the tabernacle is set up almost a year after Israel left Egypt (40:17). The same date marks a new beginning elsewhere: the waters dried from the earth on the first day of the first month and Noah removed the ark's covering (Genesis 8:13), and Hezekiah began purifying the temple on that day (2 Chronicles 29:17). Ezekiel's vision of the restored temple also begins its purification rites on this date (Ezekiel 45:18). The book ends where the calendar begins again.

a: Their anointing will make them a priesthood for all time
p: The priesthood is promised 'for all time,' yet it has had no temple since AD 70. Jews and Christians answer differently.
b: "For all time" (olam) is said of Aaron's priesthood here and of Phinehas's line in Numbers 25:13. Since the Romans destroyed the temple in AD 70, there has been no altar for the priests to serve. Jewish tradition holds that the priesthood continues in waiting: kohanim keep their identity and duties such as the priestly blessing, and many look for its restoration with a rebuilt temple (Ezekiel 44:15). Christian tradition, following Hebrews, holds that a change of priesthood brings with it a change of law, and that Christ's priesthood fulfills and replaces Aaron's (Hebrews 7:11–28). The Hebrew olam can mean "for a very long time" as well as "forever."

a: He took the testimony and placed it in the ark.
p: The broken covenant's replacement is laid in the ark, under the atonement lid, beneath the cherubim.
b: Moses himself puts the tablets of the covenant into the ark, as commanded (25:16, 21). They lie under the atonement lid, where blood will be sprinkled once a year (Leviticus 16:14–15), beneath the wings of the cherubim, where God's voice is heard (25:22). The arrangement says something about the covenant itself: the terms are kept in the place of mercy. Deuteronomy 10:5 tells the same step from Moses' side: "I put the tablets in the ark I had made, and they are still there."

a: So Moses finished the work.
p: The words match Genesis 2:2: 'God finished his work.'
b: Vaykhal Mosheh et-hammela'khah echoes Genesis 2:2, vaykhal Elohim... mela'khto, "God finished his work." The word mela'khah, "work," is the same word used for the work forbidden on the Sabbath (31:14–15; 35:2), which is why the rabbis defined Sabbath labor by the tabernacle's crafts (see the note on 31:13). The same verb marks the end of work on Solomon's temple: "the house was finished" (1 Kings 6:38), and Hiram "finished" his bronze work (1 Kings 7:40).

a: the LORD's glory filled the tabernacle
p: The glory that rested on Sinai now fills the tent. The same happens at Solomon's temple, and John 1:14 echoes it.
b: The cloud and glory that covered Mount Sinai (24:15–18) now cover and fill the tent. Ramban saw this as the point of the tabernacle: it carries Sinai's glory with the people. The scene is repeated when Solomon's temple is dedicated: "The priests were not able to stand and serve, because of the cloud. The LORD's glory filled the LORD's house" (1 Kings 8:10–11). Ezekiel sees the glory leave the temple before its destruction (Ezekiel 10:18–19) and return to a new temple (Ezekiel 43:1–5). John says of Jesus, "We gazed at his glory" (John 1:14), and in Revelation no one can enter the heavenly temple when it is filled with God's glory (Revelation 15:8).
r: 24:15–18; 29:43; 1 Kings 8:10–11; 2 Chronicles 7:1–3; Ezekiel 10:18–19; Ezekiel 43:1–5; Haggai 2:7–9; John 1:14; Revelation 15:8; Revelation 21:3

a: the cloud had settled on it
p: Shakhan, 'settle, dwell,' is the verb of 25:8, 'I will live among them.' The promise is kept.
b: The verb shakhan, "settle," is the same verb God used at the start: "They are to make me a holy place, and I will live in their midst" (25:8), veshakhanti. The book ends with that promise kept, word for word. Moses cannot enter. The man who spoke with God face to face (33:11) has to wait outside. The next book opens with God calling him in: "The LORD called to Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting" (Leviticus 1:1). The rabbis' word Shekhinah comes from this verb.

a: through all their journeys
t: A book that ends on the road
p: Exodus ends not in the promised land but on the move, with God in the middle of the camp.
b: Exodus does not end with arrival. It ends with a people on a journey and God traveling with them, the cloud by day and fire by night, as at the start of the march (13:21–22). Numbers 9:15–23 describes the system in detail. The rabbis said the sukkot (booths) of the Feast of Booths stand for the "clouds of glory" that sheltered Israel in the wilderness (Talmud, Sukkah 11b). Paul says Israel was "baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea" (1 Corinthians 10:1–2), and many Christian readers see the church as a pilgrim people led by the Spirit (Hebrews 13:14). The book's question, whether God would go among his people (33:3, 15), is answered.
r: 13:21–22; 33:3; 33:15–16; Numbers 9:15–23; Numbers 10:11–12; Nehemiah 9:19; Psalm 78:14; 1 Corinthians 10:1–2; Hebrews 13:14
